Gaming_Tech.title: Newcastle: Matthias Jaissle questions booking compared to rival managers
Gaming_Tech.text:
Newcastle United head coach Matthias Jaissle has questioned why he was booked for his touchline behaviour after he felt some other animated managers were not.

The fourth official repeatedly reminded Jaissle to stay inside his technical area during last week's 2-2 draw against Bournemouth before he was eventually shown a yellow card by referee Rob Jones in the 70th minute for straying outside again.

After the game, at St James' Park, Jaissle contested the "benefit of that rule" if he was "just supporting and engaging with the team".

"I hope I don't need to adapt," the 38-year-old said a few days on. "I was really clear that I was disappointed.

"I made that also really clear in many aspects because, from my point of view, if you're 20cm outside your box and you encourage and support your own team in a positive way, an emotional way, I'm not sure if that's then a yellow card.

"Also compare when I'm looking at some of my colleagues."

Jaissle, who arrived from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli last month, is the only manager to have been cautioned in the Premier League in the opening weeks of the season.

When asked if there were other coaches who were as animated, who were not booked, Jaissle said: "You can say so."

A new charter on participant behaviour was introduced by the Premier League, the FA, the EFL and the Professional Game Referees in 2023, which specifies occupants must remain within their technical area during the match.

In pre-season, officials from the Premier League and the Professional Game Referees visited each top-flight club to update managers on operational matters and laws.

Gaming_Tech.title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog
Gaming_Tech.text:
The UK needs new regulations for AI products used in the NHS and other healthcare settings, says Britain's industry watchdog.

The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which regulates all medical devices and licenses treatment drugs in the UK, has published 44 recommendations to update its policies as the use of AI in the sector rises.

The technology will soon be routinely used within the NHS, MHRA chief Lawrence Tallon told the BBC.

"What I would expect is that patients will... increasingly see AI as part of the way that normal NHS healthcare is delivered," he said.

"That should happen in a way that they can maintain their trust and their confidence in what's happening."

The report was compiled by an independent commission and involved input from more than 12,000 people including patients and clinicians.

The recommendations include:

Continuously monitoring AI products and removing them from regulatory approval if they malfunction or become less effective over time

Giving patients the right to know whether AI is involved in their care, and easy access to information about the products involved

The power to penalise the developers of an AI product if it fails to meet required standards

An AI "L plate" system which would make it easier for new AI models to be trialled by healthcare professionals under close supervision

"The medical devices regulatory framework predominantly dates from a period where we were thinking about things like hip replacements and knee replacements, or smaller things like stethoscopes and plasters," Tallon said.

He added while current guidelines may work for simple AI products trained to spot known symptoms on scans, for example, the rules do not apply to more complex models.

"Unlike most of the medical products we're used to regulating, these products continue to change after the point of authorization," he said.

"As new data gets fed in, they learn, they adapt, they drift."

And he acknowledged trying to regulate AI is a global challenge.

"I don't think at this moment in time we can point to a single country, a single regulatory framework, and say that they have absolutely cracked it," he said.

AI note-takers known as scribes, which are powered by LLMs, are reportedly used by 40% of UK-based GPs to record consultations and generate reports.

But a recent study from the University of Edinburgh found patients could be less likely to share personal information such as substance abuse history if they knew the conversation was being processed by AI.

Professor Henrietta Hughes, a GP who was part of the report commission, said that many of her patients were happy for AI being used during their consultations, but some chose to opt out.

"Some say, 'I don't want to talk to a robot', and that is also fine," she said.

Prof Hughes acknowledged that the scribes could make mistakes in their notes but said it was the responsibility of doctors to correct them.

While currently AI is more likely to be used to assist with administrative tasks, or carry out symptom spotting overseen by a human expert, there is a lot of excitement about its potential in the health and medical research industries.

Professor Alastair Denniston, an ophthalmologist who also worked on the report, described the technology as "an exceptional opportunity" for healthcare which was "likely to rank alongside step-changes such as antibiotics and MRI".

In September Rene Haas, the boss of chip designer Arm, told the BBC he believed the tech would come up with a cure for cancer "within our lifetime".

But there are also concerns about AI models making wrong decisions as a result of biases in the patient data used to train them, and incorrect medical advice being given by AI chatbots.

Gaming_Tech.title: Google to fund Finnish AI with €13bn investment and nuclear power pact
Gaming_Tech.text:
Google will buy up to half the electricity produced by one of Finland's nuclear power plants as part of a record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in the country's AI infrastructure, the company announced.

The US tech giant said the package would fund three new data centres, expand an existing site and support energy projects to power growing demand for AI services.

"This is Google's largest single investment in Europe and a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure," the company said on Wednesday.

"Google's decision is a clear testament to our strengths," Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement.

As part of the deal, Google signed a 22-year contract with Finnish utility Fortum to buy up to 50% of the output from the Loviisa nuclear power plant.

Earlier this week, TikTok announced a $1bn investment in Finland to build a new data centre in Kouvola, pointing to the country's "strong digital infrastructure, clean energy mix, robust data governance and skilled tech talent".

Finland has emerged as an attractive location for data centres because of its cool climate, plentiful low-carbon electricity and relatively uncongested power grid. The colder temperatures can reduce the energy needed to cool facilities packed with computer servers.

Technology companies are racing to secure power supplies as the AI boom drives demand for vast networks of data centres.

The Google investment is expected to support more than 37,000 jobs during construction and boost Finland's GDP by €3.6bn a year, according to Google. Construction is set to take place in 2027 and 2028.

"The value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment into spurring innovation, research and development," Orpo added.

"Deepening our collaboration with Google will deliver lasting benefits for both parties."

Google will build new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, while expanding its existing facility in Hamina, which it established after converting a former paper mill in 2009.

The infrastructure will help support products such as its AI chatbot Gemini, alongside services including Search, Maps and YouTube.

Google said the investments also covered "clean energy projects, and dedicated nature and community funds to support local biodiversity, education, research, and workforce development".

"Google is proud to deepen our roots in Finland," said Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet and Google.

"This investment underscores Google's commitment to grow our presence responsibly, pairing the expansion of our technical infrastructure with new energy capacity, grid enhancements, and energy affordability initiatives," she added.

Earlier this year, Google's parent company Alphabet raised its global spending plans to as much as $205bn as it sought to expand computing capacity for AI services.

The agreement with Fortum provides long-term financial certainty for the Loviisa plant, which currently generates about 10% of Finland's electricity.

Fortum said Google's commitment would support an investment programme aimed at extending the life of the nuclear station and increasing its generating capacity.

Gaming_Tech.title: Anthropic researcher believes more than 10% chance AI 'could kill all humans'
Gaming_Tech.text:
A top safety researcher at Anthropic has warned AI is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

Evan Hubinger said in a post on X, external the risk from the models which currently exist was "low" but he was "worried" the technology might develop and improve itself soon to the point where it posed an existential risk to humanity.

He did not spell out how he thought AI systems could in future result in humans being wiped out.

But his comments are the latest in a series of increasingly stark warnings about AI, with the debate shifting from whether it truly poses a risk to how big that risk is.

Hubinger's intervention was in response to another post on X, external from Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who has just quit Anthropic and previously worked at OpenAI.

"Neither company is acting responsibly," he wrote.

"These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources."

OpenAI has been approached for comment.

Dame Wendy Hall, a computer scientist who advises the UN on AI, told the BBC she was "shocked" by Hubinger and Coxon's social media posts.

She told the World at One on BBC Radio Four some of it could be "PR and marketing" however, as Anthropic and OpenAI raced towards highly anticipated stock market debuts.

But she added: "Why would someone want to say that? I would plead with investors not to invest in this company if that is their value system."

The resignation prompted Darren Jones, former chief secretary to the Treasury and chief secretary to Sir Keir Starmer, to write an open letter to Prime Minister Andy Burnham calling for a new multinational treaty for the safe development of AI.

He told the BBC governments had to come together to "collaborate" about what a treaty based on the development of superintelligence should look like.

"Unless governments take these warnings seriously enough and step up to it, the pace of development could mean that we end up with problems before we've started to look at whether it is an issue for us or not," he said.

Separately, the Financial Times reported, external Anthropic withheld its latest model from the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI), one of the leading bodies in the world for assessing AI risk.

Anthropic has declined to comment on the posts by its employees or the situation with the AISI.

A Cabinet Office spokesperson did not comment on whether the latest model had been withheld from the AISI - instead saying it "continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic, to make models safer".

In his post, which has been viewed more than 10 million times, Hubinger said "we really do earnestly believe" AI poses a species-ending risk to humans.

"I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to," he added.

Hubinger works in AI alignment, which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into the technology. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

Many leading researchers say those attempts appear to be failing, as demonstrated by a string of incidents this summer where AI agents - AI systems that are allowed to operate autonomously - carried out cyber-attacks.

OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all disclosed hacks carried out by their AI tools.

In Anthropic's safety report from August, external, it wrote there was a low risk of its models becoming misaligned with a hypothetical powerful organisation's desires, causing it to exploit or tamper with its systems.

It also said there was a similarly low risk of highly capable AI being able to "perform automated research and development" which could cause "catastrophic harm initiated by the AI". But it said it was "less confident in this assessment" than it was previously.

"We are seeing early signs of potential acceleration," it wrote.

Leading figures in the AI field have been raising the alarm about the safety threat the tech poses for years, with the heads of OpenAI, Google Deepmind and Anthropic saying as much in 2023.

But those warnings have become much more stark in recent weeks, as evidence emerges that firms may be struggling to control AI.

Earlier this month, OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki called for "extreme caution" over AI's progress, warning more intervention may be needed to ensure "humans remain in control of the future".

Major figures in the space have been calling for AI development to be slowed in recent months, including Anthropic bosses Dario Amodei and Jared Kaplan.

In an open letter signed by 1,300 staff members of AI firms, external, they called for the US government to "support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development".

Gaming_Tech.title: White House pulls Tetris-style 'Build The Wall' game after copyright concern
Gaming_Tech.text:
The White House has taken down a Tetris-style game on its website called "Build The Wall", days after The Tetris Company raised concerns over its use of the game's likeness.

The game, which saw players stack blocks to build a wall to "protect the border" is one of five arcade games which have appeared on the White House website.

On 4 September the official Tetris account on X posted, external the firm was "not involved in the creation" of the game and it took "copyright infringement very seriously".

The White House has not responded to requests for comment from the BBC or given an official reason for the takedown.

"At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and building people together, not dividing them," the firm said in its initial response to the game.

"To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we're grateful to have you in our community."

The Tetris Company has had previous success in suing firms for infringing on its copyright - settling for an undisclosed fee with the makers of the iPhone game Mino in 2012, which it claimed stole the look and feel of the block-builder.

Four other arcade games still remain on the mini-game section of the White House website.

"Flappy Bill", a clone of the 2013 viral hit Flappy Bird sees players fly a bald eagle and dodging monuments from the National Mall.

Meanwhile in Rio Run, players must "patrol the line along the river", with gameplay reminiscent of the classic phone game Snake.

Gaming_Tech.title: Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India: report
Gaming_Tech.text:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of abuse

Meta ran hundreds of paid ads with artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse imagery, including several in India, over the past 10 months, a new report by US-based campaigners has found.

The report comes two months after the Indian government ordered Meta to remove all ads and content promoting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. This was in the aftermath of a BBC Eye investigation which found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India.

Washington-based Tech Transparency Project (TTP), external says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram, the majority of them (274) in August this year.

When the BBC wrote to Meta about these findings, they said in a statement, "We don't tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated. These criminals constantly shift tactics to evade detection, which is why we keep strengthening our detection and enforcement."

The TTP report, published on Tuesday, says that it identified several photos of real children, including a member of a European royal family, that were used in the ads and then manipulated using AI. It says more than a dozen ads appeared on Meta platforms even after TTP made the company aware of its findings.

About a quarter (84) of the ads ran in India and 78 of these were published after the Indian government's order on removing CSAM and its meeting with senior Meta officials.

After the BBC investigation, several Indian agencies including the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and the National Human Rights Commission have said they are examining the matter.

The distribution of CSAM is a criminal offence in India, while Meta's policy states that ads must not contain content that sexually exploits or endangers children.

When the BBC contacted Meta about its investigation, it said that when it becomes aware of apparent child exploitation, it reports it to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in compliance with its legal obligations.

The NCMEC is the centralised global reporting system for the online sexual exploitation of children.

But Bhuwan Ribhu, the founder of Just Rights for Children, a network of more than 250 organisations working to prevent violence against children in India, says this is not enough.

Just Rights for Children has filed a petition in India's Supreme Court, citing the BBC's findings, and asked for directions to social media platforms for mandatory reporting and identification of those promoting child sexual abuse material

"Social media companies are clearly flouting Indian laws by not reporting child sexual abuse content to Indian law enforcement agencies as mandated by our child protection laws," said Ribhu.

The TTP, a research initiative of the non-profit Campaign for Accountability that seeks to hold large technology companies accountable, said it found 332 ads featuring CSAM on Instagram and Facebook running in the US, UK, EU, Australia and India. They say they have reported all the ads to NCMEC.

According to TTP, almost all the ads they found start with a photo of a child, and, as the video plays, the photo is manipulated by AI to show them engaging in a graphic sexual act.

TTP described one ad which ran in India as: A photo of a preteen girl animated so that she performs a graphic sex act, with a voiceover that says, "There are no restrictions. All the characters are real people and there are many options. This is the AI men actually use." The BBC has not seen this ad.

According to TTP, the ad was posted by more than 50 different handles in India over a fortnight in August this year.

In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post on its website, external about how it fights child exploitation on its apps.

"Anyone on our platforms can report ads if they believe they violate our policies," it said.

TTP said that it tried reporting ads via Meta's own reporting system and that of the 84 ads that ran in India, they were able to report 55. Meta only gives the option of reporting ads when they are live.

For 43 of these, TTP got a reply that said, "We've taken a look and found that this ad doesn't go against our Advertising Standards."

For 11 ads, they were told that the content had already been removed. They haven't received a response yet for one ad.

The ads that BBC had found in its investigation also directed users to another app - the messaging app Telegram - where they could buy the material for as little as 99 rupees [$1.05; £0.80].

Telegram told the BBC at the time that the company uses both automated and human moderation to tackle CSAM, and that it has "virtually eliminated the public spread of CSAM" on its platform.

Ads on Meta's platforms are only published after first being approved by its moderation technology. Its review system relies primarily on automation and is designed to check images, video, text and audio, as well as who the ad is targeting and where links send them to.

After the BBC's investigation, Meta had said that "no system is perfect" and that "determined criminals continue to try to exploit our platform, including through our advertising systems".

But TTP found that several of the ads featuring child sexual abuse were placed by Meta's own ad agency partners in China.

These partners, known as "resellers", channel billions of dollars' worth of Chinese advertising onto Facebook and Instagram. The partners did not respond to TTP's questions.

TTP said that new ads have continued to appear even after they made Meta aware of their report's findings. They shared details of 17 ads including 11 that ran in India on 1-2 September.

Gaming_Tech.title: Should promotion depend on how workers use AI?
Gaming_Tech.text:
It's in Duncan Trevithick's interest to be good at using AI at work - if he can use it to get more tasks done, faster, he'll qualify for a bonus at the end of the year.

On the surface, it's a great incentive. But he's questioning what's really in it for him.

"The uncomfortable interpretation is that employees are being assessed on how effectively they can participate in their own redundancy," says Spain-based Trevithick, 34, who works in marketing for an AI training data company.

But if he uses AI to take care of two days worth of work each week, he says the financial rewards don't add up.

"I do not receive two days off or a 40% pay rise. The higher output simply becomes the new baseline. In the short term, that may help me get promoted. In the longer term, I have helped prove how much of my job no longer requires me," he says.

"I'm just trying to view myself as a manager, and I'm managing some people, and I'm also managing AI agents, or AI loops, or whatever you want to call it."

Using employees' AI abilities as a measure of whether they should get a bonus, promoted - or even sacked - is fast becoming more common.

Accenture CEO Julie Sweet told the Rapid Response podcast in March: "Today, AI at Accenture is how we do work. So if you want to get promoted, you've got to do the things that we do in order to operate at Accenture."

And big names like Disney, Meta, JP Morgan and KPMG have introduced "AI leaderboards" to track and rank employees' usage of the array of LLMs and platforms at their disposal, according to media reports, external. Crypto trading platform Coinbase has already fired engineers who didn't complete AI training, as requested by the chief executive, Brian Armstrong, external.

It demonstrates how eager business leaders are to see a return from their AI investments, especially when 94% of companies have yet to see significant value from AI, according to a report, external by consultants McKinsey.

Employees feel they have to get on board, thanks to the current state of the jobs market - in the UK, vacancies have hit a five-year low.

Meanwhile, 75% of the 1,881 UK jobseekers polled in July by recruiter Gi Group say they would not be put off applying to an organisation that had introduced AI proficiency into individual performance reviews. Around 22% said it would be off-putting.

"It's like being in the sea and you see a giant wave coming. You can get out a surfboard and try and ride it as long as possible, or you can just let it take you under. But you can't stop the wave," says Trevithick.

But what's going on at the large consultancy Pamela (her name has been changed to protect her identity) works for isn't sitting right with her.

She's a US-based senior executive who has observed that, while there isn't a formal mandate for employees to use AI, it's obviously determining who is rewarded, and who is left behind.

"The ground is shifting under us. You've got to demonstrate [AI] fluency and fluidity as one of your key achievements. It's kind of quiet where nobody's saying, 'learn AI or else'. But let me tell you, in performance reviews, they reward who uses it well," says Pamela.

That shift, she adds, means that AI capabilities are now counting for more than actual experience, which is creating a "two tier workforce".

"You've got the same job title, same tenure, but different value based on whether someone treats AI as a threat or a tool - that gap widens really quickly once leadership notices it," says Pamela.

"AI fluency beats credentials every day. Somebody that has 15, 20 years of experience and no AI fluency will be passed over for those that have, say, three years, but are fast with the tools."

She adds: "If you're not visibly using AI, you see slower promotion timelines. It's harder to be seen, and it's harder to fight being on that shortlist."

But is it legal for companies to shift the goal posts like this?

Legally, bosses are in the clear, confirms Tina Chander, partner and employment lawyer at Weightmans. But she says it does open up questions about pay and fairness.

"The question then becomes whether the employer increases expectations on the basis that the employee can now produce more work. Is that fair?" questions Chander.

"And if an employee is effectively doing more because AI has made them more efficient, should they be rewarded differently? Or are they effectively making themselves redundant, thus acting as a disincentive to be productive?"

Chander advises businesses to have clear policies, training and boundaries in place, otherwise they risk employees opening up disputes about fairness, performance expectations and job security.

Indeed, from January 2027, UK employees will have six months to submit unfair dismissal claims compared with the current three months, and will be able to do so after just six months service, rather than the current two years.

Yet HR consultant Tina Rahman says employers aren't currently being transparent enough in telling employees why they want AI to be part of people's jobs, and what the end purpose of that is - which she agrees is to save costs and time, but also to cut down on outsourcing.

"Because they misunderstand it, this is not being reflected to employees," says Rahman, who runs a London-based consultancy, HR Habitat.

A lack of clarity around AI usage is certainly causing discontent at Pamela's company.

"Leadership is being inconsistent and vague on purpose. Firms want productivity gains without owning the disruption narrative," she says.

"If something goes wrong, they're going to say, 'I didn't tell you to do that. Where'd you get that from?' Then if you did something with AI, and it works, great."

Mandating AI use at work can become purely performative, rather than having any real positive impact, warns Kamila Miller, applied AI researcher and lecturer at Henley Business School.

"Make AI usage a KPI [key performance indicator], and people will log their interactions to hit the metric, route work through a chatbot that did not need it, and generate AI-flavoured outputs that look productive on a dashboard. You will measure adoption. You will not measure judgement, learning, or better decisions," states Miller, who is based in Reading.

"You have not made people more skilled - you have made them more obedient."

Some firms have acknowledged those arguments.

In April, Luis von Ahn, the CEO of Duolingo, told the podcast Silicon Valley Girl, external that his language learning firm is no longer using AI use as part of performance reviews.

"We found that people... were asking: 'Do you want us to use AI for AI's sake?'

"In the end we backtracked and we said: 'Look, the most important thing for your performance is that you are doing, whatever your job is, as well as possible. A lot of times AI can help you with that. But if it can't, I'm not going to force you to do that.'"

Meanwhile, in May, the Financial Times reported, external that Amazon had shut down an internal leaderboard which tracked employee's use of AI. The report said employees had been attempting to climb the rankings by setting AI needless tasks.

Despite those high-profile moves, some staff still they need to show AI proficiency - Pamela is one of those.

In her mid 50s, she plans to retire within 10 years, and wants to keep her job so she doesn't risk losing any pension and health benefits. She's visibly stepping up how AI is helping her bring in new clients, and making sure she's being credited for it.

As for Duncan Trevithick, he's doing his best to future proof himself with a number of side projects.

"If AI can do a job better than you can, it makes sense for the business to replace you. That's how the capitalist model works. So it's about, how can you move into a position where you own assets where you can leverage AI, and then you benefit," says Trevithick.

Gaming_Tech.title: OpenAI says it cracked 90-year-old maths problem in 88 hours
Gaming_Tech.text:
OpenAI says it has found a solution to a decades-old advanced maths problem in a matter of hours using a new artificial intelligence (AI) model and thousands of AI bots.

The ChatGPT-maker said on Tuesday, external that by focusing a group of roughly 10,000 AI agents, or AI bots that undertake tasks somewhat autonomously, it solved a notoriously difficult maths problem in just 88 hours.

The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, external, which concern how fluids move. For 90 years important aspects of the problems have lacked a proof, the argument underlying a correct math equation.

OpenAI called the solution which it found a "milestone" and evidence that AI tools are improving quickly.

OpenAI's solution has yet to be verified independently or publicly accepted by The Clay Mathematics Institute, a maths organisation based in the US which runs the Millennium Prize that offers big money to the first to solve certain mathematical conundrums.

But the company's claim has already sparked a backlash.

Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematics professor at New York University, said on Tuesday, external that he and Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working for OpenAI rival Anthropic, had also been working on solving the problem.

The duo had been using OpenAI's tool Codex in their work. But Buckmaster said that on 3 September, he found out that "information about our progress had been passed to OpenAI".

Buckmaster's statement came the same day, but hours before, OpenAI published its Navier–Stokes work. He claimed that OpenAI did not begin working on the Navier–Stokes equations until "after information about our work had reached OpenAI". He included text from emails exchanged with OpenAI over the work and his questions of the company's timing and methods.

Buckmaster added that he had not yet read OpenAI's full proof, but felt compelled to go public with "what I was told, when, and what was proposed to me...because the alternative is to let a sequence of announcements say something I know to be false".

OpenAI on Tuesday congratulated the "concurrent work" of Buckmaster and Alpöge, calling it "remarkable".

The company said it had not seen "any of their work through any means until they released it publicly" and that no user data was accessed in its work on the Navier–Stokes problem.

"While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models⁠", the company added. "However, our proofs differ significantly and even the precise results proved are different."

OpenAI said that, at the end of August, it started to train a new model that quickly showed that it was adept at maths. AI models are computer programs trained on huge amounts of data to recognise and predict patterns in information.

While the new OpenAI model remains a tool only used within the company, as it is "significantly more capable" than the company's most recent AI model release, its researchers decided to use it on certain notable advanced maths problems.

OpenAI admitted that last week on 1 September, it had "heard rumours that two Millennium Prize problems had been resolved" and so decided to put thousands of AI bots trained on the new internal model to work attempting to solve some of the remaining problems.

By Sept 5, or roughly 88 hours after it had set 10,000 AI bots to the task, OpenAI had found a solution to what's referred to as the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem.

The problem is at the heart of turbulence, which is a phenomenon that is still not well understood.

Although it took the AI bots seemingly little time to reach a solution, OpenAI said the bots exchanged nearly 3 million messages and used up 130 billion output tokens, or the individual lines of text and code an AI model produces in answers, on Navier–Stokes alone.

Such an effort would have cost roughly $10m (£7.3m), based on OpenAI's own pricing, external for output from its most advanced models.

The solution that OpenAI says it has now reached for the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem resolved two out of the four statements in the proof that the Millennium Prize had demanded. The prize is worth $1m to a winner.

"Our goal in releasing this result is to report on the substantial progress of our AI models," OpenAI said on Tuesday. "We do not intend to claim the Millennium Prize for this result."

Gaming_Tech.title: New law to force tech firms to prevent children from taking nude images
Gaming_Tech.text:
The government has said it will introduce a new law to force tech firms to prevent children from taking or sharing nude images on mobile devices.

Apple and Google, which develop the operating systems of most smartphones used in the UK, were given three months in June to block access to nude images on smartphones and other devices used by under-18s.

But culture secretary Lisa Nandy MP told MPs on Tuesday that despite "significant commitments" from both companies, current proposals "do not meet the scale of this crisis".

She said ministers would look to legislate "as soon as they can" - with the caveat it may reassess these if firms develop and implement solutions sooner.

Alongside making tech firms block nudity on devices used by children at device-level, the government said its draft legislation would also make providers of apps used by children introduce similar blocks on nude imagery.

"This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world," Nandy said.

She told MPs that Apple and Google had already made "meaningful changes" to block nudity on smartphones used by children at the core of their systems, but more action was needed.

An Apple spokesperson said it launched its Communication Safety feature in 2021 to help stop children from seeing or sharing imagery containing nudity - and had since "continued to expand its capabilities".

"We share the UK's commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen Communication Safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe," they said.

A Google spokesperson told the BBC it was an "industry leader in combating non-consensual intimate imagery and advancing child safety across our products".

They added Google was pleased to have "made progress" and remained committed to working on efforts to keep children safe online.

The government proposals have been welcomed by organisations and charities calling for tougher measures and technical solutions to stop children from not just seeing, but also capturing and sharing nudity on smartphones.

Ofcom data suggests that a growing proportion of younger children in the UK own a smartphone - and that the number of those do increases with age.

According to children's charity the NSPCC, content filmed on a child's device can be the starting point for grooming, sexual extortion and other forms of online child sexual abuse.

UK police chiefs have previously said restricting the ability of children's devices to take or share nude images would be a key step in preventing sextortion - crimes where a child is groomed into sharing explicit images and blackmailed.

Chris Sherwood, NSPCC chief executive, said legislative plans were a "necessary move" after tech firms failed to meet the three-month deadline.

But he said "children cannot face more delays, so Government must act swiftly and ensure these measures are enshrined in law at the earliest opportunity".

Andy Burrows of the Molly Rose Foundation said while the new proposals were "fundamental to their objective", it had been "a needlessly long and torturous road" to secure them.

"Ministers will need to demonstrate they are committed to delivering robust legislation without further delay," Burrows added.

Government proposals to prevent nude images being shared taken and shared by children were originally proposed as part of the government's violence against women and girls strategy.

But it faced criticism within its own ranks for being slow to enact it.

Its plans for a new law to enforce the measure would not prevent adults from accessing naked imagery on their device.

However, implementing solutions to block it for children may require checking whether the user of a phone, or app, is an adult or a child.

Online rights campaigners at the Open Rights Group have previously warned that implementing the change would mean "every adult would be forced through a digital ID checkpoint, and private images could be scanned by default".

The government has denied that the move would amount to surveillance.

Entertainment.title: Strictly: New hosts explain their roles as they reject 'roving presenter' reports
Entertainment.text:
Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe have said they will not have "fixed roles" on Strictly Come Dancing, as they prepare to replace Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman later this month.

Daly and Winkleman left the programme together at the end of the 2025 series.

Daly was the host on the dancefloor, introducing the dancers and judges, while Winkleman did the post-dance debrief upstairs in the "Clauditorium".

"No one's replacing anybody - at the minute it's all very kind of open," Willis told Richard Osman on The Rest is Entertainment podcast.

They also scotched reports of Radebe having a "roving reporter" role , externalon the show, with Willis saying: "There's definitely no backstage roving reporter, which is what has been reported quite a bit."

Widdicombe added that they would "be like Total Football" [where players can take the role of anyone on the team], adding: "We're going to be moving everywhere".

Radebe added he will definitely be doing "a little bit of prying and finding out the truth", having been a professional dancer on the show, with the advantage of knowing everyone on it really well already.

He called his new role "very, very exciting," although he admitted he felt a "little bit of a tinge" of FOMO [fear of missing out] at seeing the pros in rehearsals.

They also added that the plan to put the three of them together was a "wild card decision" by producers, which took them all by surprise.

Willis explained the audition process, saying they had to do a "chemistry test" to see how they interacted as a group.

She said they were told: "This is the last one and this is a wild card. We're just like, 'What happens if we do three?'

"And they said, 'It's so much of a wild card, we don't really have a script for you either.

"'So we're going to sit down, get it up on the screen and we'll have a little tinker all together'."

Entertainment.title: Drag Race UK: BBC drops Ru Paul show after eight series
Entertainment.text:
RuPaul's Drag Race UK is leaving the BBC after eight series, the broadcaster has confirmed.

A spokesperson for the broadcaster said it was facing "very difficult choices" in the face of "significant financial pressures".

The show is currently broadcast on BBC Three and iPlayer. Future series - as well as its spin-off vs The World - will be broadcast on Wow Presents Plus, a streaming platform owned by the production company behind the show.

At its peak, the UK version of the international drag competition averaged at around 1.5 million viewers per episode.

A spokesperson for the BBC said it was "proud [...] of this groundbreaking show" and thanked "RuPaul, World of Wonder and everyone involved, both on and off screen".

Started in 2019, Drag Race UK brought British drag into mainstream entertainment in the UK, and has made household names of drag performers such as La Voix, Danny Beard, and Tia Kofi.

The show sees drag queens compete in a series of challenges to impress judges RuPaul, Michelle Visage, Graham Norton and Alan Carr, and often features big name celebrity guest judges.

It has become a staple of LGBTQ+ culture and has been praised for its portrayal of the distinct style of British drag.

The corporation is currently rolling out plans to make £500m of savings, with director-general Matt Brittin previously telling staff "the scale of savings requires tough choices".

A BBC spokesperson said: "As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly."

Announcing the news on Instagram, Wow Presents Plus said a "new era" of Drag Race UK was on the way.

A new series, Drag Race UK All Stars, which sees previous fan favourites return to compete again, will premiere in Autumn 2027 exclusively on Wow Presents Plus.

BBC News understands the current series of Drag Race UK, which launched in September 2026, will continue to air as normal on BBC Three and appear on iPlayer, and all existing series will continue to be available once the move is complete.

Tia Kofi, the winner of RuPaul's Drag Race UK vs The World series 2 in 2024, stated that the programme has, until now, provided a platform for performers who otherwise lack mainstream representation.

The performer told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday that cutting the show also means a "marginalised" audience now has nowhere to go.

"I think the mistake is that they seem to be dropping programmes that they consider to be for more niche audiences, which I just don't think makes a lot of logical sense because the niche audiences are the ones who are very much staying on and watching these things," the Drag Queen and singer said.

"But particularly when it comes to programs like Drag Race UK or the cancellation of I Kissed a Boy and I Kissed a Girl, or the Rap Game UK on the BBC as well, the more marginalised audiences have limited representation in mainstream media.

"[They] offer people a platform when they wouldn't have that. There aren't really those alternatives for drag performers in the UK."

Last year's runner-up Elle Vosque told BBC Newsbeat that taking the show off the BBC where it's "accessible to everyone" would make it more challenging for people to discover drag.

"You could be flicking through the BBC and fall upon the show and end up loving it and it could be totally not something that you've been exposed to before – so I think that is the biggest downside," she said.

Fan Alex Re agrees, saying: "For that young queer kid sat at home wanting a community, wanting something to relate to, that's now behind something they have to pay for.

"It feels like we're losing that kind of access, it's a worry that kids aren't going to have that."

The BBC does represent the LGBQT+ community through storylines in shows including Mr Loverman, Rob & Rylan's Grand Tour, Amandaland, EastEnders, What It Feels Like For a Girl, The Dickie Show, Vigil, Smoggie Queens, Such Brave Girls and Juice.

The corporation declined to comment on whether future series of other international versions of the show, including Drag Race Canada and Drag Race Down Under, would continue to air.

Earlier this year, the BBC announced it was dropping LGBTQ+ dating show I Kissed a Boy - which made history as the UK's first gay dating show - and I Kissed a Girl.

Jordan Burrow, a contestant on series two of I Kissed a Boy, said the decision was an example of "where we're at within the queer community".

The corporation said at the time that it was "exceptionally proud" of the shows but they had to make "difficult choices in light of our funding challenges".

Entertainment.title: Harry Styles extends tour, with Kylie as a support act
Entertainment.text:
Harry Styles is extending his record-breaking Together, Together tour in 2027, with 25 more shows, including a return to Wembley Stadium next August.

The singer, who is currently in the middle of a 30-show residency at New York's Madison Square Garden, is adding dates in Ireland, Spain, Italy, Germany and France - who all missed out on the tour's first leg this summer.

Every city will see a different support act, with 80s pop icons Tears For Fears playing at Wembley, and pop legend Kylie Minogue on the bill in Los Angeles.

Although Minogue is a festival headliner in Europe, these shows will represent her first ever stadium concerts in the US.

She celebrated the announcement on her Instagram stories, writing: "Together, together. Harry. Me. Can't wait to see you in April, LA."

Unlike the first half of the tour, which concentrated on long residencies in cities like London and New York, the 2027 dates represent a more traditional rolling stage show.

Styles will also play US stadiums for the first time as a solo artist - with dates booked in Phoenix, Dallas, Atlanta and Chicago.

After confusion and outcry over ticket prices for the 2026 shows, the singer's team have made the pricing structure clear for his upcoming dates, specifying that prices will range from $60 to $300 (£44 to £221).

The 2027 dates will also introduce "Unpredictable Fun Tickets," an initiative to make concerts more accessible to people on a limited income.

The programme will make a limited number of tickets available for £20 in the UK, $20 in the US and €20 in Europe. Details on availability and how to apply will be announced soon.

The cost of regular tickets will vary by city. Details, including on-sale dates, are available on the star's website., external

Fans were already aware that a second leg of Styles' tour was on the way, after the 32-year-old posted a note on Wednesday teasing what he called the "final" shows of the hugely-successful run.

"When we decided to do the 2026 tour I knew it would be special but what you turned it into was far beyond what I could have imagined," he wrote.

"I love playing music, I love being with all of you and being a part of the love and joy you all create together every night. That's why I wanted you to be the first to know we will be adding 2027 dates, which honestly, at first I found daunting.

"Being an artist is the only life I've ever known really, I have been doing this since I was 16 years old, and I feel like the luckiest person in the world to still be sharing these moments with you.

"Tomorrow's announcement will be the final cities of Together, Together," he continued.

"After that, I don't know what comes next for me, but I know that I'm excited to find out."

Reviews for the Together, Together tour have been largely positive.

Rolling Stone magazine called Styles "effortlessly charismatic" , externaland noted there was "real diversity" in a setlist that covered all four of his solo albums to date.

Variety magazine was also impressed by his stage presence, external, writing: "Styles is a one-in-millions performer, with a hurricane-force charm that's dashing and sexy and goofy at the same time."

The BBC's own review noted the unique stage design, which carved Wembley into smaller fan zones, making the event "more like a club show than a stadium concert - with Styles zipping around the borders, blowing kisses and posing for cameras throughout the night".

Styles' 12-night stint at the venue earned him a Guinness World Record for the longest residency by a musician at Wembley Stadium during a single run.

He will wrap up the tour with three further nights at the stadium next August. £1 from every ticket sold in London will be donated to the Live Trust, which aims to support and protect grassroots music in the UK.

Entertainment.title: Actor Noel Clarke charged with sexual offences
Entertainment.text:
Actor Noel Clarke has been charged with sexual offences including sexual assault, voyeurism and exposure.

The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) authorised the Metropolitan Police to charge the Doctor Who and Kidulthood star on Wednesday.

Clarke, 50, from Kensington, west London, was charged with two counts of sexual assault, three charges of voyeurism and one charge of exposure. The offences are alleged to have taken place between 2007 and 2016 and relate to five women.

Clarke has not yet publicly responded to the charges.

In a statement released on Wednesday, the CPS said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and that it is in the public interest to do so."

The charges follow an investigation by detectives which began a year ago.

A man, then in his 40s, was first arrested in connection with the investigation on 25 September 2025.

A file of evidence was later given to the CPS who authorised charges.

Clarke will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 21 October at 10:00 BST.

Det Supt Mike Cagney, whose team is leading the investigation, said: "The women connected to these charges continue to receive support from specially trained officers.

"We urge anyone who has been a victim of sexual assault to contact police. The information you provide will be dealt with in the utmost sensitivity and we have trained investigators on hand to support you."

Clarke found fame playing Mickey Smith in Doctor Who between 2005 and 2010, and went on to become a successful actor, writer, producer and director.

Entertainment.title: Channel 4 to cut 340 jobs by the end of the year in major shake-up
Entertainment.text:
Channel 4 has said it plans to cut 340 jobs before the end of the year, reducing its workforce by more than a quarter.

The network, which broadcasts Gogglebox and The Great British Bake Off, will lose around 28% of its current 1,270 staff following a strategic review of the organisation.

Priya Dogra, Channel 4's chief executive, said the announcement "marks the first phase of our transformation, ensuring Channel 4 is the right shape and size to deliver its future strategy and focus investment in the programmes audiences love".

Caroline Dinenage, chair of the culture, media and sport committee said the news would be "deeply worrying for the talented and dedicated people who work at Channel 4".

The network said it planned to focus on creating a simpler and more efficient operating model and enable greater investment in distinctive programming.

In her statement, Dogra said: "Channel 4 is a precious asset which plays a unique role in the UK.

"We need to secure and own our future so we can continue to make shows others won't, reach audiences others can't, and thrive as a distinctive and disruptive British voice for future generations.

"The challenges we face require a fundamental transformation in how we work. I know the proposals we are announcing today will be very difficult for many colleagues and will have a significant impact across the organisation."

She added: "These decisions have not been taken lightly, but I strongly believe they are necessary to create a simpler, more focused and more sustainable Channel 4."

Entertainment.title: South Park creators rename show 'South America' in apparent dig at Trump
Entertainment.text:
The creators of South Park, the animated TV show, have announced that its new series will be named South America, in an apparent reference to US President Donald Trump's attempts to rename a lake and a gulf.

"Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA," creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker wrote in a statement.

Trump signed an executive order in August to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and last year declared that the Gulf of Mexico be known as the Gulf of America.

The announcement from South Park, now in its 29th season, comes after the show won an Emmy for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday.

It's not yet known whether the new name will be adopted permanently, or if it will revert to South Park later in the series.

The name change shared to the show's official social media account featured an image of the South Park sign with the word 'Park' replaced with 'America'.

"We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount - a Skydance Capitulation," its creators said in the post.

Paramount Skydance is the show's parent company. The Trump administration this year approved a $111bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery - one of the biggest media deals in history.

But the merger has since been paused until June 2027, after 12 US states filed lawsuits against the deal for fear of it harming competition and leading to higher prices for consumers.

A day before the show's announcement, Trump shared an AI-generated video of him placing the word 'America' over 'Mexico' on a "Welcome to New Mexico" sign.

In August, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, Trump ordered a similar change for Lake Ontario - renaming it Lake America.

Apple and Google subsequently changed the name in their respective Maps apps for US-based users.

And last year, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed as Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.

South Park, which has run since 1997, has regularly mocked the US president during his two presidency terms.

Both its creators, Stone and Parker, have repeatedly drawn criticism from Trump, the White House and MAGA supporters for its jabs at the president.

During its 27th season, the White House described South Park as a "fourth-rate" show that was "hanging on by a thread with uninspired ideas in a desperate attempt for attention", after an episode depicted Trump naked in bed with Satan.

After winning the award for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday, South Park also shared an image depicting a fictionalised Donald Trump with the words: "You finally got your Emmy."

The new season of will premiere on 16 September.

Entertainment.title: Family of murdered teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial
Entertainment.text:
The family of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez has lobbied for the death penalty if D4vd is found guilty murdering their daughter.

D4vd, who was born David Anthony Burke, is charged with killing the teenager, whose dismembered body was found in the trunk of a Tesla car registered to his address on 8 September 2025. Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

The death penalty is under a temporary ban in California, where Burke is due to stand trial, but in a statement Hernandez' family said execution "would be perfect" if the singer was convicted of murder.

In a related development, Hernandez's parents filed a civil lawsuit against Burke on Friday, seeking monetary damages including burial and funeral expenses.

The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple, external US media outlets, external, makes similar claims to those raised by prosecutors in the criminal case against the singer.

Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas allege that Burke caused the wrongful death, false imprisonment and childhood sexual assault of their daughter.

In the court documents, they say Burke and Hernandez first met in November 2023, when she was 13 years old.

Over the next 16 months, they claim, the pair would exchange almost 10,000 texts and have sex several times.

"At all relevant times Burke was an adult who occupied a position of authority over decedent, a minor, and was able to and did exercise undue influence and control over her," the parents say, in papers filed last Friday.

They go on to claim that Burke killed the teenager at his Hollywood Hills home, when she threatened to reveal their relationship, after allegedly sending a message that read: "I will end ur career and ur life".

In addition to Burke, the lawsuit names several of Burke's companies and managers, his mother and a live-in security guard.

Hernandez's parents allege that these people "enabled Burke to isolate" Rivas Hernandez and facilitated his travel, housing and security.

Burke's management company Mogul Vision and finance manager have previously denied knowing about Burke and Rivas Hernandez, the Los Angeles Times, external reported.

In July, a judge found enough probable cause for Burke to stand trial on the murder charge in the criminal case. At the time, the district attorney said he was weighing whether to seek the death penalty.

In a statement on Monday, which would have been Hernandez's 16th birthday, her family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution.

"If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter," read the statement, released via the family's attorney.

Burke again pleaded not guilty to the charges last week and has since parted ways with his celebrity defence attorney. He is now being represented by a public defender and is due back in court on 19 October. His trial has been moved to next year.

Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel has said that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence".

"We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said.

His office did not immediately provide comment on the civil lawsuit.

Entertainment.title: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader Reece Weaver swaps boots for Broadway
Entertainment.text:
Former Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader Reece Weaver has shelved her cowboy boots and swapped the football pitch for the stage as she steps into one of the most famous roles in the world.

Weaver was a breakout star of the Netflix docuseries America's Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, with her exit from the squad a major storyline of the third season.

Making her Broadway debut in the musical Chicago, she faced criticism that it was her profile, more than her talent, which landed her the role.

After much fan speculation, she officially stepped into the role of murderess Roxie Hart this week at New York's Ambassador Theatre.

"The audience loved her," says Sealy Sikes, who attended the opening night with her mum Tammy Pack.

Her mum's a big fan of the Netflix series, which follows the cheerleaders through gruelling auditions and training regimes as they compete for their spot dancing in one of the world's best known squads.

Sikes says she was less familiar with fan favourite Weaver before the curtain went up and was impressed with how she commanded the stage.

"She did a great job, she's a very big, charismatic actor.

"It was a little bit shaky at the beginning, but if I wasn't hyper aware that it was her first time, I wouldn't have even thought anything about it."

Clips shared on social media showed the audience erupting in applause for a grinning Weaver as she took her first bow.

But the decision to cast a celebrity - known as stunt casting - meant Sikes was "nervous" for Weaver and whether she could translate her skills from the football field to the stage.

"Her strong suit is the acting and dancing," says the 28-year-old.

"She's a great singer but of the three talents that's probably not her strong suit, relatively speaking.

"But even then, she was great."

And while stunt casting is criticised for taking roles from actors, Sikes says it might actually be a positive thing for long running shows like Chicago, which is the longest running show on Broadway.

"If that's something that gets people back in the seats and re-interested in a classic that has to just continuously fill out that auditorium, then I would say that's a good thing."

When her casting was confirmed, Weaver said it was one of her "biggest dreams as a performer" to be on Broadway.

"I cannot believe this dream has come to fruition," she said in a TikTok post, which has since been viewed more than six million times.

Mickey-Jo Boucher is a theatre critic and content creator and tells Newsbeat that stunt casting is needed to "interest ticket buyers", especially for shows that might be "slowing down at the box office".

But at the same time, he recognises why it's not always popular.

"We don't want it to become so widespread that established theatre actors and the real talents of the theatre world are missing out on opportunities or that it's to the detriment of the calibre of these shows," he says.

"Because at the end of the day the most important thing is that the quality of the show is the highest that it can be."

Chicago's choice of Weaver isn't the first time a production has picked a celebrity star.

Earlier this year, rapper Megan Thee Stallion was cast as Zidler in Moulin Rouge!, becoming the first woman to play the role of the nightclub boss.

Although she quit the show early, her performance received strong reviews and boosted interest in the show, with fans reportedly travelling from across the US, external to see her.

Six The Musical also booked Grammy-winning singer Abigail Barlow and content creator Dylan Mulvaney for a run of shows back in January.

"When a show starts to struggle a little bit more, they tend to use celebrity casting," says Boucher.

"By being there, they're actually keeping a lot of other people employed at the same time."

Reece's role has already attracted her fans to Broadway, with some like Samantha Milo waiting to meet her at the theatre's stage door on her debut night.

"I do think there is some stunt casting involved, however she is a great addition regardless," the 19-year-old tells Newsbeat.

"She earned her spot there, she has been dancing and performing her whole life, this was a big goal for her."

"Having Reece step into the role helps new fans who may never have thought to go and see Chicago, find a way to enjoy the show."

The production runs for six weeks until 18 October.

Entertainment.title: Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price
Entertainment.text:
After taking a fallow year in 2026, the Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's event will go on sale in October.

Tickets for the weekend will cost £408 including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from 2025.

Headliners for the festival, which takes place from 23 to 27 June, have yet to be announced, but rumours are already swirling, with everyone from Harry Styles and Fontaines DC to Taylor Swift and Stevie Wonder said to be in the mix.

Tickets for the festival typically sell out in less than an hour, with thousands of fans joining online queues to fight for their place.

In a post on the official Glastonbury Instagram page, external, organisers said tickets with coach travel would go on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday, 1 October.

General admission tickets go on sale a couple of days later, at 09:00 BST on Sunday 4 October.

As part of an ongoing campaign to stop touts, anyone wanting to attend Glastonbury had to be registered in advance. You can check your registration on its website. , external

In recent years, the festival has also introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.

Glastonbury, which features more than 100 stages, was already the UK's most expensive music festival, but next year's ticket prices are the highest ever - breaking the £400 barrier for the first time.

The increase is part of a pattern across the industry.

Analysis by BBC News found the cost of attending the UK's major festivals has surged over the past decade - rising above the rate of inflation.

Parklife tickets have increased by around £69 (71%) in real terms since 2013 - while Reading and Leeds had a much smaller increase, rising by about £40 (14%) over the same period.

In the same period, Glastonbury's ticket prices went up by about £85 - a 30% price hike.

Entertainment.title: Don’t sashay away! The BBC’s decision to cancel Ru Paul’s Drag Race UK is sickening in all the wrong ways
Entertainment.text:
The BBC is canning RuPaul’s Drag Race UK – a decision that, in my household, will bring the number of regularly watched programmes on the Beeb down from one to zero. It’s a decision that will no doubt please enemies of LGBTQ+ culture, but otherwise seems inexplicable. For a start, Drag Race UK regularly pulls in 1 million viewers a week, which hardly seems like a show in its death throes (even if this is down from a previous high of 1.5 million).

RuPaul’s Drag Race is also a bona fide cultural phenomenon. Since the US version started in 2009, it has brought tons of performers to national, or even global, attention who would otherwise still be plying their trade in provincial gay bars. Jinkx Monsoon from the US is now starring in Oh Mary! in London’s West End; the UK’s La Voix made it on to Strictly; and Bimini Bon-Boulash, who “stepped their pussy up” to astonishing effect in season two, has made records, modelled and written a book.

More importantly, the show gave a TV platform to ballroom culture – the New York City-born tradition in which impoverished, young, largely Black and brown gay men and trans women, usually ostracised by their families, formed their own “houses” and transformed themselves into the glamorous characters they dreamed of being. Ballroom culture gave the world vogueing, the documentary Paris is Burning, and a whole argot which, more than 30 years on from its popularisation in the film, is mainstream. “It’s giving”, “she’s serving”, “throwing shade”, “spilling the tea”, looking “snatched”. We’ll never know what the queens who invented this lingo would think of its incredible resilience, since they perished in the Aids crisis.

RuPaul’s Drag Race UK fused this underground culture with Britain’s venerable drag tradition to often hilarious effect. Who could forget characters like the acid-tongued, high fashion queen A’Whora from season two, whose comedy routine was so filthy it managed to make judge Alan Carr wince? Or Cheddar Gorgeous, the historically minded and hugely articulate queen from season four, whose Act Up themed costume I last spotted on display in Manchester’s Whitworth gallery? Or even Nyongbella from season seven, delightfully random and usually almost naked, strutting her stuff on the BBC in defiance of her disapproving relatives in Cameroon, where gay sex can get you a five-year jail sentence? In what other context would such characters have made it on to the BBC?

That’s not to mention the amazingly high-profile celebrity guests (Andrew Garfield, Mel B and Michaela Coel have all served), and the always-fabulous judges Michelle Visage, Graham Norton and Carr. There is also, of course, the positive impact on scared young LGBTQ+ people on seeing out gay and trans folk living their best lives on screen, working – or rather werking – hard and being unapologetically themselves. Isn’t that something worth preserving?

Along with the girl group challenges, Snatch Game episodes and spectacular looks, Drag Race UK has seen its contestants discuss their experiences of being non-binary or living with HIV. And while, as a cynical Briton, I often cringe at the climactic moment when the queens who make it to the final talk tearfully to pictures of themselves as children, it’s a reminder that self-acceptance is something many LGBTQ+ people still struggle to achieve, especially in the midst of the current global backlash against our hard-won rights.

Prudes and homophobes might say that BBC licence-payers don’t want to pay for a bunch of drag queens telling filthy jokes and bitching about one another on the small screen. Well, I also pay the TV licence fee and I do. It doesn’t seem much to ask that, as a gay person, I get one programme on iPlayer that is unabashedly queer – especially since the BBC also canned I Kissed a Boy and I Kissed a Girl for bad measure. As the arts editor of the Guardian, I guess I could watch the BBC’s amazing slate of arts programmes – were it not for the fact that most of them have also long been chopped.

Drag Race UK has an ardent fanbase of all backgrounds and generations. Of course, not everyone in the LGBTQ+ community likes it – Travis Alabanza’s play The Sound of the Underground entertainingly railed against it – but it has expanded its definition of drag considerably, featuring trans and one female performer among the legions of cis gay men. A contestant in season one even had a girlfriend at the time – and if that’s not inclusion, what is? BBC, RuPaul’s Drag Race UK should not be allowed to sashay away.

Entertainment.title: Alex Winter: ‘Michael Winner was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met’
Entertainment.text:
You were born in London but grew up in America. When do you feel most British? DonarudoToranpu

The UK is still my second home. I’ve worked there a lot as an adult. When I’m back in London, I like walking on Hampstead Heath, so I would say that’s where I feel most at home.

Having played Marko in The Lost Boys and then John Polidori in Haunted Summer, have you been tempted to take on another vampire-related role? And was getting staked to death while you were sleeping a bit of a disappointing end for Marko – what would have been your preferred way of going out in style? Death by stereo, perhaps? Finbarre and MoreorLesPaul

I’d love to do another vampire movie. I love those characters. They’re interesting and great fun to play. There are some really good vampire movies – I’m grateful I was in one that has, for some reason that none of us can figure out, really stood the test of time. And I love Marko’s death. As an actor, the first time you get staked is the most memorable.

Which Keanu Reeves was the most fun to work with: in Waiting for Godot on Broadway; as Ted “Theodore” Logan to your Bill S Preston, Esq in Bill & Ted; or as mutant Ortiz the Dog Boy when you directed him in Freaked? And following Waiting for Godot, what wildly inappropriate classic should Bill & Ted tackle next? FioreSebek and GunHarp

I just love performing with Keanu. The funny thing is we both play bass, so all through the first Bill & Ted, whenever we weren’t shooting, we’d be jamming. Keanu and I both have theatre backgrounds and have studied Shakespeare, so I’d like to do some Shakespeare, maybe something like Measure for Measure. There’s a few that we’ve discussed. I’m not sure if we’ll get there, but who knows? Never say never.

My kids (six and nine) have just discovered Ben 10 in all its incarnations and I saw you directed the live-action versions. If you could choose the powers of any of the aliens in the Omnitrix, which would it be and why? LethalLiaison

Heatblast was my favourite. He’s a powerful fire character. My children were obsessed with Ben 10 at the time, and we worked on those together, which was something I don’t often get to do, so it was a lovely experience. I met my wife on that project too. She was running Cartoon Network studios at the time.

Michael Winner directed you in your first film, Death Wish 3. Say something nice about him – and where did you go out drinking when you were filming it in London? ExFi and OttoMaddox

I can absolutely say something nice about Michael Winner. He was the most erudite sociopath I’ve ever met. That’s a compliment. We used to drink in Brixton, largely. One of the people working on the show – I think he may have been involved in some criminal activity, so maybe the less said about him the better – owned a club there. They would close it and we would hang out there all night. I was 19 when I made Death Wish 3. It was a very fun, formidable summer.

You’ve made documentaries about Napster, the dark web, blockchain and YouTube. Which part of the internet scares you most these days? Zenchi

The hasty, greed-oriented rush into the AI space is the most frightening thing happening right now. That’s not to say all AI is bad, but a lot of the people running the AI companies are very bad. So what scares me the most is the tech oligarch takeover that’s occurring in so many areas of business, politics and civic culture.

After directing your Frank Zappa documentary, for those, like me, who’ve been immune to his charms, can you recommend a Zappa track or album? HenleyRegatta

I didn’t make the doc as a big fan. I made it because I was very interested in Frank Zappa as a way into looking at American culture and artistic culture. He’s a really good doc subject: someone who decided to live their life in a purely artistic way, and what the consequences of that were. If you want the quintessential Zappa album – unless you are just never going to like him – it’s impossible not to enjoy Hot Rats. I’m also very partial to the album he made at the very end of his life, The Yellow Shark, which is almost a classical, jazz-oriented album.

The Bill & Ted movies feel like a beautiful, optimistic tribute to the idea that music created by ordinary people will save the world. Do you think it still could? venusdenico

I do think that good art will always help the world. It’s not the only thing. But I do think that music and other art forms absolutely help the planet and help humanity.

Thanks for that wonderful ending to Bill & Ted Face the Music. Will there be a Bill & Ted 4? brucevayne1000

Keanu and I would love to make a fourth movie. I think the stars have to align in a number of areas for that to happen. But we love playing these characters. We kind of are Bill and Ted. We started playing the characters so young, I don’t really think they exist without us. We defined the characters from the very beginning, so I don’t think it really matters how old we are. It becomes a question of how long can you act, and I think one can act until one is no longer breathing. I really hope they don’t do a reboot. I don’t really want anyone else to play Bill, because I am Bill. That would be a disaster.

If you had access to Bill & Ted’s phone booth, which non-bogus historical figures would you visit? TeeDubyaBee

I would like to go back to ancient Greece. I would love to meet Euripides or Aeschylus. Or go to Shakespeare’s time. The future too. What is going to happen? Will there be a planet? I’d be curious to go 40 or 50 years into the future and have a look at whether we pulled ourselves out of this climate disaster we’re falling into, which I believe we will. I’m not a nihilist. But I’d be curious to see how we did it.

If you could “melvin” anyone in real life – as Bill & Ted do to Death in Bogus Journey – who would it be? Dr_J_A_Zoidberg

I grew up in the US, and I did not grow up with “melvin”. I grew up with “wedgie”. It must be a coastal thing. Maybe on the west coast they say “melvin”? In the midwest and the east coast they definitely say wedgie. Anyway, who would I most like to melvin or wedgie? Elon Musk.
