articles.title: Oil prices rise above $100 a barrel for first time since July as Iran war escalates
articles.text:
The price of oil has risen above $100 a barrel for the first time since July as the escalating conflict in the Middle East threatens further disruption to global supplies.

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by more than 3% to top $101 after tensions increased in the Gulf amid the latest tit-for-tat exchange of fire between the US and Iran.

The US military said it had “destroyed” multiple Iranian tankers, after Tehran attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles. The previous nightm Iran-backed Houthis attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze.

UK and mainland Europe gas prices also soared on Wednesday. The benchmark Dutch gas contract rose by almost 4% to €78.73 a megawatt hour, the highest since January 2023. Meanwhile, the British contract rose by 7.77p to 196.57p a therm, the highest since December 2022.

On Tuesday, the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, said the latest rise in oil prices was putting pressure on inflation and interest rates. “The risks, I’m afraid, are on the upside,” he told MPs. “And that’s really the risks coming from energy prices.”

The oil price has jumped by a quarter since early August as hopes for a permanent resolution to the six-month-old war faded.

The climb in costs has hit UK motorists, with petrol at the pump reaching an average of 166.2p a litre on Tuesday, the highest level in four years, according to the motoring body the AA.

The AA said diesel hit an average of 187.7p, a price it last reached in May. Prices for a litre of petrol have risen 4.4p since the August bank holiday, with diesel up 4.1p.

Households will face further pressure on their bills when Ofgem’s energy price cap rises by 4% in October. Andrew Goodwin, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Oxford Economics, has predicted that the cap could now rise by a further 13% in January.

“Wholesale prices are currently well above the level of the previous observation window, and our commodities team expect them to remain high in the near term,” he said.

The energy companies BP, Shell and the British Gas owner, Centrica, were among the top performers across the FTSE 100 on Wednesday morning, with their shares rising by at least 1% on the back of the higher oil price. The index was down by 0.5% overall.

Brent is up more than 60% this year, and has risen above the $100 mark for three periods so far in 2026.

China, the world’s largest importer of crude, has increased purchases in recent days, after a hiatus that had been a factor keeping oil prices somewhat in check in the early part of the conflict.

Giovanni Staunovo, a commodity analyst at UBS Global Wealth Management, said: “For the direction of crude prices, we are also monitoring Chinese crude imports as a key indicator.

“Chinese crude imports recovered to nearly 9m barrels per day in August, up from the June low of 7.15m, but still lower compared to the [pre-conflict] February imports of 12.6m. It looks like the recovery trend could continue.”

Oil prices have fluctuated in the six months since the start of Tehran’s block on the strait of Hormuz prompted what many feared would be the greatest energy supply disruption in history.

In the first weeks after the first US-Israeli attacks on Iran in late February, oil prices soared past $100 a barrel. The oil price peaked at $126 in April but later fell back amid hopes of a ceasefire. The price then began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and hostilities restarted.

The rise in energy prices has stoked fears about inflation and the prospect of higher interest rates this year. In the US, economists are expecting at least one interest rate rise from the Federal Reserve by the end of the year.

articles.title: Electronic shelf labels likely to cost jobs and drive up grocery prices, US report warns
articles.text:
The universal adoption of electronic shelf labels in grocery stores across the US could cost tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in lost wages while further driving up grocery costs, according to a report released on Tuesday.

An analysis by the AFL-CIO Tech Institute of the label manufacturers’ own marketing materials found the universal adoption of electronic shelf labels, which are marketed to retailers as a cost-cutting measure, could cost workers between $1.6bn and $6.9bn in lost wages annually and affect between 44,223 and 191,633 jobs.

The policy brief – Priced Out, Pushed Out: Electronic Shelf Labels Raise Prices and Shrink Paychecks – calls for a ban on electronic labels to protect consumers and workers.

Manufacturers have hailed the labels as a way to collect huge amounts of personal data from customers, increase profits and cut labor costs.

The report argues that electronic shelf labels use the same pricing systems that allow dynamic pricing – price changes such as increasing allergy medication prices when pollen counts are high – to surveillance pricing, changing prices based on personal data.

These technologies are being implemented across the US retail industry at a time when food prices have surpassed inflation and wage gains, increasing 33% over the past seven years.

“Through our analysis, we found that the implementation of electronic shelf labels are likely going to drive prices even higher. The reason being that these labels are connected to the same algorithmic pricing software that online retailers are already using,” said Sunny Glottmann, policy and programs managers at the AFL-CIO Tech Institute and co-author of the report.

“Electronic shelf labels create the infrastructure that would make rapid algorithmic price changes easier to implement at scale, and this raises concerns for consumers that are already struggling with grocery costs.”

The report comes as several states have begun introducing legislation to ban surveillance pricing and electronic shelf labels. In April, Maryland became the first state in the US to ban surveillance pricing. Connecticut signed a ban into law in June and New Jersey signed a ban into law in July.

Electronic shelf labels “enable instantaneous price changes”, said Lauren McFerran, executive director of the AFL-CIO Tech Institute and former chairman of the National Labor Relations Board.

“This is a technology that both is enabling this kind of ‘how do we extract the absolute most money out of grocery shoppers that is humanly possible’ and ‘how do we squeeze our workers as much as is humanly possible’,” said McFerran.

A May poll released by the United Food and Commercial Workers union found 68% of Americans believe surveillance pricing will increase grocery costs and 65% say digital price tags will do the same. About 67% support banning digital price tags and surveillance pricing, with only 26% opposing a ban.

Ademola Oyefeso, vice-president of UFCW International, said that as retailers are implementing electronic shelf labels, the labor cuts occur gradually, with workers who typically change prices on shelves losing work hours.

“Slowly, if someone has a full-time job or a part-time job, they go from full-time to part-time, from part-time to no time, and that’s what’s going to start happening across the entire industry,” said Oyefeso. “We have gone with paper labels for over 100 years. It’s worked. It’s the trust stores have built with people. I know [that] you and I are paying the same price.

“If we come there on Monday, you and I are going to pay the same price on Monday, on Tuesday, on Wednesday.”

Oyefeso said workers were also consumers, and that electronic shelf labels allow price changes to occur multiple times a day.

In December, Instacart ended a pilot program practice that allowed retailers to charge online shoppers different prices for the same products after an investigation by Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found grocery prices could differ by as much as 23% between customers.

“ESLs are the embodiment of surge pricing and surveillance pricing,” Oyefeso said. “Shelf labels allow grocery shopping to become airline ticket shopping.”

articles.title: US bans Canadian dairy, alcohol and motorcycles as trade war escalates
articles.text:
The US is banning dairy products, most alcoholic beverages and motorcycles from Canada, the White House said on Tuesday, as the trade war between the two neighbors and longtime allies escalates.

The ban will take effect in three weeks and comes after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on $20bn in US imports earlier on Tuesday.

Donald Trump also moved to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term US government contracts as Canada’s retaliatory tariffs took effect and the prime minister, Mark Carney, vowed to speed efforts to reduce the country’s dependence on the United States.

The US president directed the General Services Administration to declare Canadian products ineligible for those contracts until Canada allows “full and fair reciprocity″ for American products.

Carney said on Tuesday that Canada’s strategy was about becoming more independent. “It’s about ensuring that no country can hold us hostage. And that we can live how we want to live.”

The rupture has upended one of the world’s closest relationships. On 22 August, the US imposed 50% tariffs on about 5% of Canadian imports, charging that Canada had unfairly treated the American dairy, alcoholic beverage and auto industries.

The US and Canada have long sparred over trade, particularly Canada’s protected dairy market and the US government’s allegations that it subsidizes producers of softwood lumber. But they remained friends and staunch allies.

Under Trump, US-Canada relations have deteriorated rapidly. In addition to imposing tariffs on Canadian products, Trump has repeatedly made inflammatory comments about making Canada the 51st US state. Carney came to power in a come-from-behind political victory last year by promising to stand up to him.

Some Canadian provinces have banned the sale of US alcoholic products – a move that prompted the retaliatory US ban on Tuesday.

How the trade war ends could carry consequences far beyond Canada, testing whether a smaller US ally can resist Trump’s economic pressure without being forced to yield.

Earlier on Tuesday, a Canadian official said Ottawa did not intend to change course regardless of whether Trump responded with nothing or what the official called a “nuclear response”.

The government’s strategy will remain focused on building more at home and diversifying trade abroad, the official said.

The tariffs hit hundreds of American products, including steel, aluminum, cheese, appliances, clothing, cosmetics and farm equipment, at rates of 15%, 25% or 50%. They cover about $20bn in American goods, roughly 6% of the $333.6bn the United States exported to Canada last year.

Since Canada-US trade talks collapsed 21 August, Trump and his administration have imposed additional tariffs and issued a series of threats and attacks portraying Canada as weak and dependent.

Trump’s trade war and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have fueled anger across the country. Canadians have sharply cut travel to the United States and boycotted US goods, moves Carney praised as signs of national resolve.

Gabriel Brunet, a spokesperson for Canada-US trade minister Dominic LeBlanc, said officials from both countries remain in contact even though formal talks have not resumed.

articles.title: Catherine joins Prince William at suicide prevention campaign
articles.text:
The Princess of Wales has made a surprise appearance alongside her husband the Prince of Wales, as he gave an impassioned call to the sports sector to help prevent suicides.

"Sport can help save lives," Prince William told sports players, mental health charities and sports industry figures at Everton's football ground in Liverpool.

He was launching a project that wants to use sport to help open conversations and end the stigma surrounding mental health.

"Sport has the ability to reach people who may never walk through the door of a mental healthcare service," he said.

The On Your Side project wants to give people confidence to start the "difficult conversations" with friends, relations, teammates or colleagues who might be struggling with their mental health and might be at risk of suicide.

It is being supported by sport stars including England football captain Harry Kane, retired British middle distance athlete Dame Kelly Holmes, and former England football star Alan Shearer.

Royal sources said that Catherine wanted to attend to "highlight the difference that can be made when people feel able to talk openly about how they are feeling and when someone is there to listen".

"Never underestimate the difference that you can make," said Prince William, stressing that suicide prevention was "not someone else's responsibility". "It belongs to all of us," he said.

Talking of hidden anxieties, he added: "We do not always see what is happening behind closed doors, or understand the battles that may be taking place beneath the surface."

Dame Kelly talked of her own struggles: "We talk about suicide, which is the end for that journey. What we forget is that journey has happened for a long period of time. What we need to avoid is that journey coming to that endpoint."

It was important that sports stars admitted their own vulnerability, said Olympic cyclist Dame Laura Kenny.

She spoke movingly of how a family member had tried to take their life and how she felt "almost ashamed to admit that this could happen in my family because it's not a subject that is easily spoken about".

The cyclist also described the darkness of her feelings after the loss of two babies, through a miscarriage and an ectopic pregnancy, "which ultimately ended up in an emergency situation".

On Your Side aims to use the reach of sport to raise awareness about suicide and to show people the help available in a crisis, with the Football Association, Premier League and Team GB providing support.

The level of suicide is disproportionately higher among men than women - it is the biggest cause of death for men under the age of 50 in the UK - and sport is seen as an effective way of communicating that help is available.

"My hope is that every sporting organisation in the country will look at what is being launched today and ask a question: 'What more can we do?' Because the opportunity before us is enormous," Prince William said.

The royal couple saw a bench at the ground dedicated in memory of Gary Speed, a footballer who once played at the club, and who died by suicide in 2011.

The bench, unveiled last year, is intended to give people a space to speak openly about their anxieties and the royal couple met Speed's mother there.

Shearer was a friend of Speed and is backing the call for people to try to support people they have worries about.

"You don't have to be an expert. You don't have to have all the answers," said Shearer. "But we can all be better at asking, listening, and helping someone find the right support."

The project has been created with the British Standards Institution and mental health charities, including Chasing the Stigma, which has an app called Hub of Hope which has a directory of places to get help.

The charity's founder, Jake Mills, said he had faced his own mental health challenges and saw sport as an effective route for this type of message.

He said sport was a "real force for good" in bringing people together and for "looking out for one another".

Mark Bullingham, chief executive of the Football Association, said he wanted to see sports organisations "creating a culture where conversations about well-being are really encouraged. Where people feel comfortable asking for help and also know where to get it".

Prince William has been a longstanding campaigner over mental health and preventing suicide, with his Royal Foundation having last year launched the National Suicide Prevention Network.

If you have been affected by the topic discussed in this article, support is available via the BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Mikel Arteta close to signing new contract with Arsenal
articles.text:
The perception of Arsenal's transfer window varies depending on who you speak to - but there will be no disagreement from anyone at the Emirates Stadium over how crucial their next expected signing will be.

With the market closed until January, the club are now in the process of finalising an agreement with manager Mikel Arteta over his protracted new contract.

Well-placed sources indicate those discussions have moved forward recently amid full confidence from those involved in talks that the Spaniard will renew.

Indeed, Arteta moved unequivocally last month to remove any lingering doubt over his future: "Everybody feels comfortable that the timing of the contract is not going to be an issue because my will certainly is to be here and I'm very happy here.

"My feeling from the club is the same one. That's why everyone is doing things in a very organic way."

Similarly, Arsenal's chief executive Richard Garlick has said it was merely a "matter of time" before Arteta's new long-term deal was confirmed.

Arteta can expect to become one of the best paid managers in world football once his new contract is signed - Arsenal committed to significantly improving on his current deal, worth £10m a season plus an extra £5m upon Champions League qualification.

For Arsenal supporters, the official announcement can't come soon enough, particularly given his current deal now has just nine months left to run.

Since his appointment in December 2019, Arteta has transformed Arsenal from a club that had lost its Champions League status to one that won the Premier League for the first time in 22 years last season.

They are overwhelming favourites to retain their domestic crown and are fancied to win their first-ever Champions League this season.

With that success comes power. Like Arsene Wenger before him, Arteta is categorically the most influential figure, certainly from a football perspective, at the club.

People will say that the manager or head coach should always be the most authoritative figure at any football club - the reality is that is rarely the case.

Arteta's fingerprints are all over the club - and most importantly the squad. Nothing happens from a first-team perspective without his approval.

When Arsenal tried to sign Julian Alvarez and Vinicius Jr last month, it was Arteta who was at the forefront of the club's charm offensive.

With that in mind, the thought of removing Arteta from that dynamic, certainly for Arsenal's ownership, is the unthinkable.

One day, Spain will come calling - and a return to his homeland may attract Arteta, although he knows he is unlikely to be afforded the same authority at either Real Madrid or Barcelona – clubs that are historically entrenched in internal politics – than he is now.

But at this moment, the attraction for Arteta is with Arsenal.

This is a squad that has flourished under Arteta's tutelage. The average age of the squad (26.2 years) is one of the oldest in the Premier League. It's a group at its peak and primed to build a legacy on.

Beyond the new financial terms and into footballing ambition, Arsenal are buying into Arteta's vision.

The summer arrivals of Bruno Guimaraes and Ezri Konsa were sizeable investments given both turn 30 next year, while the albeit failed pursuits of Vinicius Jr and Alvarez provided Arteta with evidence that the club's American owners are willing to spend heavily on elite talent.

It's the sort of ambition Arteta is understood to have made clear he wanted to see as talks over his contract progressed.

Arteta's six years at the Emirates already makes him the longest-serving manager in the Premier League and EFL by some distance - his new deal will take him closer to a decade in north London.

Yet there appear to be no signs of Arteta taking his foot off the gas.

articles.title: Should Chelsea be stripped of 2016-17 title and Tottenham crowned champions?
articles.text:
Should Tottenham be retrospectively crowned Premier League champions for the 2016-17 season?

That's the opinion of former manager Mauricio Pochettino, who led Spurs to a second-place finish - seven points behind Chelsea - that season.

This is about Chelsea making £47m in secret payments, according to a Premier League investigation, to unregistered agents and third parties to seal transfers between 2011 and 2018.

The transfers included Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o, Willian, Ramires, David Luiz, Andre Schurrle and Nemanja Matic.

Four of those - Hazard, Willian, Luiz and Matic - were at the club in 2016-17.

During that period Chelsea won two Premier League titles (2014-15 and 2016-17), two FA Cups (2011-12 and 2017-18), the EFL Cup (2014-15) and the Europa League (2018–19).

Chelsea have been fined by Uefa, the Premier League and the Football Association, but Pochettino thinks that is not enough.

"If they admitted they broke the rules, the Premier League title was for the second-best team," Pochettino said.

Pochettino is one of the first people of significance to articulate what many feel - that Chelsea got off lightly with a fine.

Fans of Everton and Nottingham Forest have pointed out that their clubs faced points deductions for relatively small profit and sustainability breaches, while Chelsea sought to sign star players with secret payments.

Meanwhile, there is no sign of a verdict in the case of Manchester City's 115 charges for alleged breaches of Premier League financial rules.

Does Pochettino have a point? And how much of an impact did those four players have on the title race?

Hazard is seen as the poster boy for Chelsea's breaches.

The Blues fought off most of Europe's top clubs to sign him from Lille for £32m in the summer of 2012.

Between May 2013 and August 2016, according to the investigation, seven payments totalling £5.6m were made to an unregistered agent "for the benefit of the club in connection with Hazard's transfer".

Pochettino's argument is that Spurs could have beaten other clubs to the signing of players of similar ability had they also ignored the rules.

What about Hazard's impact in the 2016-17 season?

It was considerable.

The Belgium forward started 36 Premier League games, scored 16 goals and provided five assists. Only Cesar Azpilicueta started more matches, and only Diego Costa netted more goals (20).

Hazard was Chelsea's player of the year, was named in the Professional Footballers' Association (PFA) team of the year, and made the shortlist for PFA player of the year.

Then there's the direct impact of his goals and assists in the results of four fixtures.

Hazard scored the first goal in a 2-1 win over West Ham in August, then scored a goal and provided an assist in a 2-0 victory over Southampton in November.

In March he scored the opener as Chelsea again beat the Hammers 2-1, and got both goals in a 2-0 win over Manchester City in April.

You could argue that input was worth 10 points.

There is no doubt that Hazard had a huge influence, but this was his fifth season at the club. It was not as if Chelsea signed him in the summer of 2016.

Willian joined Chelsea from Anzhi Makhachkala in 2013, with the investigation finding that transfer fee payments totalling £19.2m were made to two unregistered entities in connection with his move and that of Samuel Eto'o.

Willian was not a regular starter in 2016-17, with 19 of his 34 appearances coming from the bench.

But he still had a huge influence, scoring eight goals and providing eight assists.

The Brazilian's attacking returns were crucial in four matches.

He had an assist in a 1-0 win at Sunderland in December. He scored two goals in a 4-2 victory over Stoke in December, and the first goal as Chelsea beat Stoke 2-1 in March. He provided an assist for the winning goal in a 4-3 victory over Watford in May.

His contributions helped Chelsea take eight points from those fixtures.

Crucially, Chelsea nipped in at the last minute to sign Willian from under the noses of Spurs, who might argue that was only because of the secret payments.

The investigation found that Chelsea made payments totalling £5.1m between 2012 and 2015 "to provide talent identification services in certain European countries".

This was identified as payments in relation to the registrations of Ramires, Luiz, Schurrle and Matic.

However, by 2016-17 Matic and Luiz were in their second spells at Chelsea. The deal with Benfica which meant Matic and Luiz swapped clubs in 2011 was looked into.

Matic returned to Stamford Bridge in 2014, with Luiz having a spell at Paris St-Germain from 2014 to 2016.

While the deals that took the players back to Chelsea were not specifically referenced, the association was created.

Matic played 35 league games in 2016-17, including 30 in the starting XI. He scored one goal and set up seven.

Only one of those attacking contributions influenced a result, but that was an assist for Chelsea's first goal in a 2-1 win over Tottenham in November.

Luiz, who was named in the PFA team of the season, started 33 matches and scored one goal - the opener in a 1-1 draw at Liverpool in January.

Tottenham were relentless at the end of the 2016-17 season, winning 12 of their final 13 matches to finish on 86 points.

Yet Antonio Conte's Chelsea were almost as relentless, winning 11 of their last 13 to take the title with 93 points.

Spurs' tally would have been enough for the title in 2015-16, when Leicester finished on 81.

However, since 1999-2000, when Manchester United were champions on 79 points, 86 points would only have won the title twice, including the two most recent seasons.

Tottenham's problem in 2016-17 was too many draws at the start of the campaign. Despite an unbeaten 11-game start, only five of those were victories.

Chelsea lost more matches - five to Spurs' four - but secured 30 wins to Tottenham's 26.

Pochettino might argue that the attacking influence from Willian and Hazard proved the difference, with those two players having attacking contributions in eight different matches which led to points.

Then there is the mere aspect of sporting advantage - how the signings of players like Hazard enabled Chelsea to win trophies, qualify for the Champions League and therefore attract more top talent.

Pochettino feels he should have a Premier League title to his name.

Remember that he managed Chelsea for one season, when he struggled to win over supporters.

Chelsea finished sixth in 2023-24, but neither Pochettino nor the club are likely to look back fondly on that period.

It is different at Tottenham, with the Argentine still adored for his five-year spell in charge from 2014.

As well as finishing as Premier League runners-up, he took the club to the Champions League final in 2018-19.

The 86 points earned in 2016-17 is a club record too.

So do Spurs fans share his view?

"Of course I do," said Chris Paouros, co-founder and co-chair of Proud Lilywhites, external and Women of The Lane., external

"He could tell me the moon was made of halloumi and I'd nod along.

"The Spurs 2016-17 team was the best in the league by most measures: best attack, best defence, fewest defeats, unbeaten at home in the last season of the old White Hart Lane.

"If the playing field was tilted, the least you can do is ask the question."

Paouros knows Spurs will not be handed the title, but said the "rules have to mean something, whoever benefits".

There is another side to this, however.

If you get given a title a decade later because of a rule breach, could you celebrate it?

"It would still be something that Spurs fans would celebrate," said Tristan Foot, secretary of the Tottenham Hotspur Supporters' Trust. "A victory over Chelsea, albeit 10 years after the event."

But that sense of injustice is still there for other Premier League clubs.

"It means that to an extent crime does pay in football," Foot said. "And that's the serious underlying part all of this.

"During the transfer window they were signing players that we had no chance of winning, the obvious example being Willian.

"The Premier League has got to be better about imposing sporting sanctions and making sure that its rules actually have teeth."

With all investigations now concluded, it seems unlikely that Pochettino - or anyone else - will get a retrospective trophy parade.

Will clubs get that same feeling when the Manchester City saga is finally over?

articles.title: Alice Kinsella: British gymnast continues historic comeback at international level
articles.text:
Olympic gymnast Alice Kinsella says "it's hard to put into words" how she feels about returning to international competition as her groundbreaking comeback to the sport continues this weekend.

The two-time European champion became the first British artistic gymnast to resume elite competition after giving birth, when she finished fourth in the beam at the British Championships in March.

Now the 25-year-old is preparing for her first competition back in Team GB colours at a senior team international against France, Switzerland, Germany and Italy at Fenton Manor in Stoke on 12-13 September.

"It's kind of crazy - it's such a surreal feeling but I am very excited," Kinsella told BBC Radio Stoke.

"It's only been a year, postpartum. Training-wise, it's been tough, but it's been good. I'm excited to finally get out there. I'm ready, I'm doing everything I can to get back where I was.

"It's been a rollercoaster but a good one."

Kinsella's pioneering journey back to the sport is so rare it became the subject of a university research paper into elite gymnasts resuming their careers after giving birth.

Her son Parker, who was born in September 2025, is already a source of inspiration and he will be watching his mum compete at the weekend as Kinsella competes in all four pieces of apparatus - balance beam, bars, vault and floor - for the first time.

"It's really special because I've wanted to try to get back into a team and this is a really good start because it's a little four-way," Kinsella, who trains with Park Wrekin Gymnastics Club in Shropshire, said.

"It's not too big of a competition which is really good. I'm definitely nervous, but it's hard to put into words - it's been so long.

"I did the British [Championships] in March but only did beam and that's all I was training really but now I'm trying to do all four so it's more on the body.

"It's not like you've done one piece and you can stop thinking about everything, you've got to move on to the next and think about that. So it's been tough."

After revealing she only took "three or four weeks off" after giving birth, Kinsella returned to training at the start of the year with the longer-term intention of being at the World Championships in China in 2027 and the Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028.

But, after finding herself ahead of schedule so far this year, she wanted to take the chance to step it up.

"My main goal was to try to get back next year but I'm actually a lot further forward than I thought I would be," added Kinsella, who won bronze in the team event at the Tokyo Olympics in 2020.

"So that's why I'm doing this competition because I just want to get out there, compete, because I don't like doing nothing."

What makes Kinsella's return so unique are the obvious challenges - and changes to the body - pregnancy and childbirth brings.

There are many examples of women returning to the top of their sports after becoming mothers but gymnastics, where vital pelvic floor and core strength are both weakened during pregnancy, is different.

Kinsella said her gymnastics background has played a big part in her being able to return to physical exercise so quickly but said she "didn't feel too bad" when she got back in the gym.

"I always had that goal to get back into the gym and I think when I've got a goal set I will do everything I can to achieve it," she said.

"Getting back into a leotard with how my body's changed just feels very weird but I guess that shows what my body has gone through and I try to think about it in a positive way."

Her body is not the only thing that has changed with Kinsella adding that parenthood has helped her become better at taking the pressure off herself as an athlete.

"Having a baby changes your life - I'm very patient, whereas before Parker I was not patient at all," she said.

"When I made one tiny mistake I would get so annoyed, but now if I just make like a little mistake I'm totally fine about it.

"You have to be patient with kids, they're crazy. So I've definitely changed in that aspect but style-wise and gymnastics-wise like I don't think that's changed.

"Things are harder to get back and to do but I think the more I train it'll probably feel a lot easier."

Kinsella said when she started her comeback "no one really had any idea what I was going to able to do" and wants to keep levels of expectation for her international return as realistic as possible.

For her, this weekend in Stoke is there primarily "just to enjoy it" and to "get the experience of all four pieces [of apparatus] again".

"My body's changed, I can't do the same amount of training I used to do but I'm definitely getting back to that," Kinsella said.

"We're definitely on the right track to be where I was before I had Parker. My goal was to start competing next year properly on all four.

"It's going to be really fun. Whatever happens, happens, good, bad. I'm just proud I'm able to be back out there a year postpartum."

articles.title: Six Nations: World Rugby offers to help switch fixture to USA
articles.text:
World Rugby would help any nation which wants to switch a Six Nations match to the United States, as it continues its drive to spread the game stateside.

South Africa and New Zealand have sold out the 71,000-capacity M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore for Saturday's fourth and final Test in their Greatest Rivalry series.

With the men's and women's Rugby World Cups being held in the United States in 2031 and 2033 respectively, tournament organisers are keen to bring more prestige fixtures across the Atlantic.

"In terms of the match-day economics, [South Africa vs New Zealand] is like a Six Nations match," Alan Gilpin, World Rugby chief executive, told the Daily Telegraph., external

"It starts to show that [financial return] is not the barrier. So if there is the appetite to take some of these big matches in the future to the US, we can now."

The All Blacks have been at the forefront of rugby's attempts to make an imprint in a notoriously tough sports market.

Ireland memorably beat the All Blacks for the first time when the teams met in front of a capacity 60,000-strong crowd at Chicago's Soldier Field in 2016, with a 2025 rematch proving a similar commercial success.

New Zealand have also staged matches against the United States - a 104-14 victory in front of about 40,000 fans in Washington, external - and Fiji - a 47-5 win before 33,217 in San Diego - in the country over the past decade

However Gilpin believes that the history of the Six Nations and its ability to connect with expatriate fans in the United States could be a useful tool to crack America further.

"This isn't a live discussion of an Italy vs Ireland game, but why we use that as an example?" he added.

"You've got two fantastic fanbases in the US of Irish and Italian fans

"If you could take a Six Nations game to the right place, to a Boston or to a New York, where there's a lot of those fanbases, you can definitely drive the economics.

"Now, you're going to have Irish fans and Italian fans in those respective home countries saying, 'Hang on a minute, you know, we want to see our country play?'

"The counter-argument to that [is] it's still Irish and Italian fans getting the chance to watch their team, so they're just not the ones who live in Ireland and Italy on this occasion. But that's a balancing piece we've got to work through."

Wales played their home matches at London's Wembley Stadium during the 1998 and 1999 Six Nations while the Principality Stadium was being built, but such a long-haul venue switch would be unprecedented in the tournament's 143-year history.

England women's head coach John Mitchell, who led the United States' men's team earlier in his career, said he was unsure whether a stateside expansion would ultimately succeed.

"I've worked for America. I understand that geography," he told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"American sport is full of rivalries and I just don't think Americans adjust to new rivalries or new franchises compared to probably some of the other countries.

"Will rugby ever go big there based on its its early investment?

"I'm not sure I can answer that, but what I do know is that rugby union is a difficult challenge for large parts of America."

He was also wary of the prospect of a Red Roses' Six Nations match being staged in the United States.

"The visibility's huge here in the European market," added Mitchell.

"Let's use it because that's the way to grow the game slowly, rather than putting huge investments into something that might have potential, but not necessarily that visibility."

While World Rugby could support a stateside Six Nations game, the decision would lie with the competing teams, all of whom would be aware of the consternation that would come with transplanting a fixture thousands of miles away.

The schedule for the 2027 editions of both the men's and women's tournaments have already been set.

articles.title: Gainsborough Trinity condemn person claiming to be manager Russ Wilcox
articles.text:
A non-league club have condemned a person who has been approaching players to make transfer and wage offers while falsely claiming to be their manager.

Gainsborough Trinity, who play in the Northern Premier League Premier Division - in the seventh tier of English football - say the individual has contacted "a number of players" across different levels of the non-league pyramid.

Chief executive Matt Boles said he wanted to make it "categorically clear" communication over potential deals had not been from manager Russ Wilcox or on behalf of the club.

"We strongly condemn the actions of the individual responsible," he said on the Gainsborough club website, external.

"Impersonating a football manager and making false representations to players is completely unacceptable and has the potential to cause unnecessary disruption and reputational damage to players, managers and clubs."

Boles said Gainsborough became aware of the bogus approaches when managers, players and officials at other clubs contacted Wilcox directly, suspecting he was not behind the phone calls and messages.

BBC Sport understands an agent also reached out to Wilcox to share their suspicions after the imposter offered them an excessively high transfer fee for a player.

"Many have done so precisely because they know Russ, know the professional standards by which he conducts himself, and immediately recognised that this is not the manner in which he would approach or attempt to recruit a player," Boles said.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Aryna Sabalenka, Jessica Pegula, Coco Gauff & Elena Rybakina make up historic semi-final line-up
articles.text:
"Oh, wow".

That was Coco Gauff's surprised reaction when she learned she was part of a US Open semi-final line-up the like of which has not been seen in more than half a century.

For the first time since 1975, the top four seeds in the women's singles draw have reached the semi-finals at the New York major.

Now, 51 years later, the stars have aligned once again with Aryna Sabalenka, Elena Rybakina, Jessica Pegula and Gauff all surviving three-set thrillers to create a semi-final line-up for the ages.

"How amazing - it doesn't get much better than that does it?" former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"It has felt fantastic the whole tournament - I just feel like I've been more enthused about looking forward to the match-ups this Grand Slam than any I can remember."

It is the first time the top-four ranked players have reached the women's semi-finals at any Grand Slam since Wimbledon in 2009, and it hints at a shift away from the unpredictable landscape that has characterised the women's game in recent years.

Since the start of 2020, there have been 13 different Grand Slam women's singles champions - compared to just seven on the men's side.

"I just feel like there's lots of really big names now, big personalities going up against each other and it's really exciting," Croft said.

"We've been blessed with the amount of intriguing matches we've had. You're seeing these warriors out on court."

Top seed and two-time defending champion Sabalenka will face American Pegula in Thursday's first semi-final (00:00 BST, Friday), while Rybakina - who will replace Sabalenka as the new world number one on Monday - takes on fourth seed Gauff afterwards.

While Sabalenka is bidding to become the first woman since Serena Williams in 2014 to win three successive US Open titles, Pegula is the only player remaining in the women's draw still chasing a maiden Grand Slam.

The pair need no introduction to each other, having faced each other 13 times.

That includes the past two US Open tournaments, when Sabalenka denied Pegula a first major title in the 2024 final and fought back to win in last year's semi-finals.

"It's fun to look at it like a rivalry. I think that's what motivates me," said Pegula.

"I know that she's definitely pushed me to become a better player, so I always respect and appreciate that aspect of our rivalry."

Pegula, who has got the better of Sabalenka on four occasions on the WTA Tour, said beating the four-time major winner at Grand Slam level is a "hurdle" she must overcome.

Sabalenka, meanwhile, said she was "super excited" to face Pegula, who arrived in New York in better form after reaching the final in both Washington and Cincinnati.

"I'm loving playing against her because it's a battle, because it's a fight, and I love being under pressure and going through tough challenges," said Sabalenka, who is into her first semi-final since falling to Pegula at June's Berlin Open.

Pegula added of Sabalenka: "I know she hasn't maybe had the best results this summer, but I know that she has a lot of confidence playing here at this tournament, and she's going for a three-peat."

By reaching the semi-finals, second seed Rybakina will become the new world number one on Monday - ending Sabalenka's 99-week reign at the top.

But the second seed has described the top ranking as "just a number" and stressed that her focus remains focused on winning her third Grand Slam title.

"It's never quite the same if you become world number one having lost a Grand Slam final or semi-final just beforehand, so she will be trying to cap off an absolutely perfect couple of weeks by winning the title," tennis correspondent Russell Fuller said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

Standing in her way, however, is Gauff, who will have the home crowd's backing on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The 22-year-old American, who won the Flushing Meadows title in 2023 but suffered fourth-round exits in the following two years, said she has a different perspective to this year's tournament.

"Sometimes you're just so focused on the now, now, now, because you want it now, and obviously you want to take advantage of your opportunities," she said.

"In the grand scheme of things, [I'm] definitely sitting here in a different mindset and perspective than I was last year.

"It inspires me a little bit more to keep working, as I see how much I have improved in a year."

Gauff leads the head-to-head 2-1, but Australian Open champion Rybakina fought back from a set down to triumph in last month's Canadian Open semi-finals.

"I'm going to have some aces hit on me and some winners hit on me, but I'm going to keep fighting and give it my all. That's all I can do," Gauff said.

articles.title: Spanish Grand Prix 2026: Can football-obsessed Madrid embrace F1?
articles.text:
You could never accuse Formula 1 of shirking a challenge.

Who else would consider competing for the attention of a football-obsessed country, home to the World Cup winners, in a city where a constant stream of the world's most talented players do awe-inspiring things most weeks?

F1 last had a Spanish world champion 20 years ago and there hasn't been a race in Madrid since 1981.

Does F1, which has experienced a huge rise in popularity in other territories around the world, need another track in its crowded European heartland?

This weekend the sport, and Madrid itself, will find out.

Real Madrid are considered to be the greatest football club in history.

They have won 15 European Cups and 36 La Liga titles, and then there are the famous Galacticos: the generational set of the world's best players which began with the likes of Zinedine Zidane and Ronaldo and has extended to the modern crop that includes Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappe.

Some 75,000 Madridistas roared home Mbappe's majestically deft volley to make it 3-0 after half an hour against Malaga at the end of August, and their city rivals Atletico aren't far adrift of them in La Liga. It's hard to see what else the locals need to sate their sporting needs.

But in both the stunning, newly reconditioned steel spaceship of the Bernabeu, which has lost none of the drama of its frighteningly steep theatrical terracing, or Real Madrid women's atmospheric if less salubrious stadium right next to the new F1 track, will fans be turning their attention to the roar of the engine noise this weekend?

"Yes, [the F1 race] is good for Madrid," says one. "There is pride in our sport, Madrid is an open city with open people and open minds.

"The race can [take] Madrid's [identity] outside of football, and the most we can be seen [by the outside world] is the best.

"But I'm more than excited… I'm curious - I want to see how it goes."

"We've always been dreaming of having something [from F1] closer to home," adds another. "Having it back is great. I've been to Barcelona and the Belgian GP and I think let's see how it goes. Organising tends to be messy in the first year - I don't want to be the guinea pig.

"Let's hope it brings the city more into the spotlight. Madrid has a lot to learn from F1 about how to run a global spectacle; F1 could probably learn the true Spanish way. Barcelona is more international, the drivers and fans coming to Madrid will get more of a taste of Spain."

As the Prado museum demonstrates, Madrid knows its fine art.

The crossing signals resemble birdsong and the Mexican conifers gently sway over the waiting traffic with a backdrop of stunning Palaciosian architecture, which is in contrast to the relatively flat, block layout of the inner city.

This may not have made for the best race experience so instead, organisers plumped for what outsiders may see as an unloved expo area run by the quasi-state owned Ifema organisation next to the city's airport.

"It started as a joke, it was a fantasy," says Luis Garcia Abad, Madring boss and former manager to Spain's only world champion Fernando Alonso, among other Spanish sports stars.

"An F1 grand prix is like a unicorn - you are trying always to see the unicorn but at the end you realise [sometimes] it's impossible.

"The queue of cities trying to organise an F1 GP is huge. They have to choose right - we signed a contract for 10 years.

"Maybe seven or eight years ago we talked about this race. At some point Ifema called me and said 'what are you thinking [about its viability]?' After one morning [here] I said: 'It's possible.'

The new venue may be a world away from the flamenco-inspired boutiques and wine bars of the intimate Salamanca district, but Madrid is relatively diminutive compared to other high-profile capitals, and has high-quality public transport.

As a result, organisers are cutting out many of the car parks and asking fans to leave their own motors at home.

But don't expect Patrick Dempsey, Rafael Nadal and Mbappe to be standing on the platform of Avenida de America to hop on the pink line to the circuit – they will breathe easy at the VIP spaces near to the expansive six-strong VIP area paddock.

Regardless of the journey there, what will fans find?

"It's a real experience, not just to be in Madrid but for F1," says Abad. "Every part of the track has its own personality. Monumental… Turn 12, is huge, amazing.

"We really wanted to have an iconic part of the circuit – more than 30,000 people around one corner."

Ah yes, Monumental. The corner everyone in F1 is talking about when discussing this race.

A 26-degree banked challenge, substantially longer than the one at the Dutch Grand Prix's Zandvoort. Monumental scythes through what will feel like a small town come race day.

It comes complete with a VIP viewing area that could house the King of Spain and his family and sits, appropriately, like a castle on top of the hill. The corner itself is a difficult structure to walk up, and in 44C heat, the tarmac is impossible to sit on.

"Luis wanted to think of something recognisable in our circuit. Something iconic," says operations director for Ifema Carlos Jimenez.

Monumental was not the only complex part of a track build, which Jimenez says lends itself to sustainability. Power for the race comes from renewable energy and there is partial use of existing buildings around the site. However, additional construction around the circuit has seen 65m euros of investment, and the track itself cost 85m euros alone.

"There were a lot of challenges," he says. "We started building it in the wettest winter in 20 years in Spain. The rain was torrential. We suffered a lot, and had to stabilise parts of clay which behaves badly with wet conditions. It was very challenging. There are three layers of asphalt here. We learnt from one layer to the next.

"In 2022 it seemed like a little bit of a crazy idea," adds Jimenez. "But Madrid has momentum right now; it's a vibrant city, very well known for football.

"Like a ski resort must have entertainment for apres-ski, a circuit must have good after-race entertainment. Madrid will become in top position - the offer of this city is incredible in terms of gastronomy, a spectacular climate, which is very mild in September. And the party in Madrid is unbeatable."

Make no mistake, Madring is a street circuit: part public roads, part purpose built. And it feels intense to stand on the track, let alone drive it, with the walls on either side appearing to close in on you. And that lack of width, on the eye at least, suggests overtaking will be virtually impossible.

"From a driver's point of view it's quite a harsh circuit," says an excited Abad. "Twenty-two corners, up and down, banking corners - the circuit is adapted to the new [F1] regulations.

"I spoke with Charles Leclerc and he said it was an amazing track, and in the race I believe you will have the opportunity to overtake, but not by free. We're talking about gladiators – the best drivers in the world."

Plenty of drivers have already experienced Madring in anger during a Formula 3 test.

"It's going to be really edgy," says Madrid's own F3 driver Bruno del Pino. "You are always on the limit, the corners are quick and the walls are close. It's like [Saudi GP circuit] Jeddah but with more difficulty.

"With Monumental, you see so much of an angle it never ends. The first time around, you see it going straight up and you feel like you'll fly straight out [of the track].

"It is flat for us because of the downforce so it's not really a corner, but the previous combination of Turns 10 and 11 are high speed and close to the wall - quite a few drivers will kiss the wall."

Britain's F3 driver Freddie Slater goes even further: "A lap of Madrid is so exhilarating, and the adrenaline is pumping - it's an incredible track to drive. It's one of the best tracks on calendar, if not the best.

"It's got character, it's got bumps, uphill and downhill – it's a bit more old-school."

Abad believes it's the spectators who will determine this race's success.

"Not just Madrid needing F1, maybe even F1 needing Madrid," he concludes. "We're investing money to create an experience inside of a city.

"The future of the [F1] championship is something in this direction – we need to take care of customers and spectators. They are our future."

articles.title: Anthony Gordon: Why Barcelona chose him over Marcus Rashford
articles.text:
Barcelona sporting director Deco says Anthony Gordon's style was a better fit for Hansi Flick's side than Marcus Rashford's as the club strengthened their squad this summer.

Rashford scored 14 goals in all competitions while on loan at Barcelona last season, who won La Liga and the Copa del Rey.

Barcelona had the option of signing the Manchester United forward on a permanent basis this summer for £30.3m (35m euros) at the end of his 12-month loan.

However, the Spanish giants decided to not extend the 28-year-old's contract and he returned to Old Trafford.

Rashford's England team-mate Gordon and Manchester City midfielder Rodri were Barcelona's two most expensive signings during the summer transfer window, and Deco says both arrivals addressed important weaknesses in the squad.

Gordon joined the Catalan club from Newcastle United in a deal worth more than 80m euros (£69.3m), saying he had believed he would play for Barcelona since he was "three years of age".

Speaking to Catalan radio station RAC1 on Thursday, Deco praised Rashford for his contribution last season but explained why Barcelona ultimately preferred Gordon.

"We are extremely grateful to Rashford," Deco said.

"He contributed a lot last season, but our idea of play is much more linked to Anthony's. His style fits with what the coach is looking for."

Deco said Barcelona had identified a lack of energy when Raphinha was unavailable last season and believed Gordon could address the problem.

"In the case of Gordon, we saw that he was one of the figures we needed," he said.

"When Raphinha wasn't on the pitch, the team lost energy and with him we could solve it. The big advantage we had is that the player wanted to come and he was able to put on pressure [at Newcastle to be allowed to leave]."

Deco added that Barcelona had analysed a number of wingers before deciding on Gordon.

"We had a clear idea what we're looking for," he said.

"We needed more intensity. We analysed a lot of wingers. Signing someone from the Premier League is almost impossible, but [Flick] was clear with what he wanted and we worked on a deal from there."

Gordon has made five appearances for Barcelona and has made four assists.

The club have won all four of their La Liga games, scoring 17 goals and conceding just two.

articles.title: Maye’s ‘unacceptable’ trio of interceptions help Seahawks win season opener over Pats
articles.text:
Backup quarterback Drew Lock led two late scoring drives and the Seattle Seahawks intercepted Drake Maye three times in the fourth quarter to overcome an early injury to starter Sam Darnold and beat the New England Patriots 13-10 on Wednesday night in a Super Bowl rematch.

The Seahawks were held to just a field goal through three quarters as Lock and the offense struggled to move the ball after Darnold injured his hip on the opening drive.

“At this point, we are able to rule out a fracture,” Seattle head coach Mike Macdonald said after the game. “So there’s some more tests to be done. ... We’re still working through all that, but right now I think fracture is out, which is great news.”

The costly interceptions by last season’s MVP runner-up turned the tide and made sure that the banner-raising night would end in happy fashion for the boisterous home crowd.

Maye overcame the first two picks to drive the Patriots into position to tie or take the lead in the final minute. But Josh Jobe made a toe-tapping interception in the end zone to seal the win.

“I thought we had a good plan to try to start chipping away and be patient. Lost patience and it cost us – decisions that cost us the game on my part, on my end,” Maye said. “I vow to myself to be better and realize it’s a long season. But at the same time, you can’t have those. It’s unacceptable.”

Seattle trailed 10-0 but got a field goal in the third quarter and tied the game when Lock connected with Jaxon Smith-Njigba on a 45-yard pass on fourth-and-1 following an interception by Nehemiah Pritchett.

Julian Love intercepted Maye on the next drive and the Seahawks took a 13-10 lead on a 26-yard field goal by Jason Myers. That set the stage for the defensive stand on the final drive.

The game started following a ceremony that featured the Super Bowl banner being raised and highlights being played on the video board. This was the third Super Bowl rematch in Week 1, with it last happening in 2016 when Denver celebrated its title with a win over Carolina.

The excitement turned to worry quickly as Darnold came up limping following a third-down sack by Dre’Mont Jones on the first drive. Darnold went immediately to the sideline medical tent and then back to the locker room before the next drive.

Lock, who threw just three passes last season, entered the game but Seattle’s offense was stagnant until the fourth quarter.

The Patriots didn’t fare much better on offense but got the only score of the first half after Jobe interfered with offseason acquisition AJ Brown on a deep flea-flicker pass and Maye found rookie Eli Raridon for a two-yard score on the next play to make it 7-0.

A penalty helped set up the second Patriots score as well. Chazz Surratt was flagged for roughing the punter on the opening drive of the second half, setting up Andy Borregales’ 50-yard field goal.

articles.title: Angel Reese and Caitlin Clark celebrate their ‘chemistry’ as USA advance to Fiba World Cup semis
articles.text:
Angel Reese and Caitlin Clark’ s interactions are a subplot of the women’s Fiba World Cup, the WNBA season and if you spend enough time on social media, a divided United States. Clark and Reese have shown their relationship on the court is thriving, and they both excelled in USA’s 108-56 quarter-final win over Hungary on Thursday.

In Thursday’s game, the growing chemistry showed. The pair had a nifty pick-and-roll to end the first quarter that ended with a layup by Reese. The Atlanta Dream forward returned the favor hitting Clark on a fastbreak for an easy lay-up later in the game.

“She’s got it for me a lot of times so it’s probably finally due for me to get one to her and she easily finished it,” Reese said smiling.

Napheesa Collier was USA’s top-scorer with 19 points, Clark delivered nine assists and added 10 points, while Reese had six rebounds and nine points in a dominant quarter-final performance. The Americans, who are chasing a fifth consecutive World Cup title, will face either Spain or Australia in the semi-finals on Saturday.

Clark and Reese are intense and animated competitors, and their fan bases’ are fiercely loyal. On much of social media fans are either for Reese or for Clark. But the pair have bonded so far at the World Cup. Clark said many of the stories about their relationship are “false takes,” saying she loves the fiery competitiveness that she and Reese share.

“No matter what, there’s always going to be people that create those narratives and say whatever they want to say,” Clark said. “There’s definitely no stopping that and they’re always going to be there. I think for ourselves, like I said, it’s easy for us to just come in here and compete.”

Reese has enjoyed playing with Clark as well as the other young members of the roster, including Paige Bueckers and Aliyah Boston.

“We know each other’s game like the back of each other’s hand, she knows my spots,” Reese said of Clark. “We just continue to build chemistry because we know we’re going to be USA teammates for a while.”

Clark laughed recalling one incident in the tournament between she and Reese that has gotten some attention. When Clark was subbing in during the opener against China and started to step on the court before being officially told to, Reese, who was entering the game at the same time, pulled her back off the court.

“Well, the ref had gotten mad at me a couple of times prior, so she was saving me from the ref getting mad at me again,” Clark said, laughing.

The pair will be back on opposite sides soon enough – Reese’s Atlanta Dream and Clark’s Indiana Fever are headed for the WNBA playoffs and both have 26-14 records. They could meet in the first round if the current seeds hold.

articles.title: Two forehands, no backhands: meet the US Open’s fascinating ambidextrous experiment
articles.text:
Teo Davidov always has the upper hands. An amiable junior prodigy from Denver, the 16-year-old was the oddest sight at this year’s US Open, the only player in the tournament – man, woman or junior – who hits only forehands. To be clear: it’s not that he doesn’t have a backhand or can’t hit a backhand. He’s ambidextrous and so he doesn’t bother with them.

It’s nothing personal. “To be honest, I like the traditional backhand-forehand,” he says. “I like the classiness of it. I like hitting backhands myself just to play around, just for fun.” He hits those from both wings, too.

Davidov has been a giddy curiosity for hardcore tennis fans for the past five years, with rubberneckers gaping at clips from his matches and training sessions that seem at a glance like AI. A four-year-old video of him flummoxing Carlos Alcaraz’s younger brother makes for especially tasty viewing. “I don’t really look at the comments or things like that,” Davidoff says. “But I’ve heard most people online just always have something they think might not work.”

Davidov’s internet clips don’t do him justice, though. You have to see him in person, especially now that he’s a 5ft 7in teenager. His second-round doubles match on Wednesday evening had hordes of wine and Honey Deuce-sipping casuals drifting over to Court 6 at sunset for a closer look – and whipping out their phones from the first warm-up ball. It really was the damnedest thing watching him alternate hitting groundstrokes with his right and left hand, lobs and volleys too.

But witnessing the kid serve was the trippiest experience by far, like watching AI in the wild. It’s always advantage Davidov. It doesn’t matter which side of the baseline he sets up on – if you’re returning, you’d better mind your backhand. “Obviously it depends on who I’m playing, but the general foundation is right hand on the deuce side and left hand on the ad,” he says. “I’ve been mixing it up a lot more, different spins, different looks, just making it as hard as possible.”

It all seems like parlor tricks, the sort of thing that could hinder him and his partner, fellow American Tyler Lee, as much as their opponents, Brazil’s Guto Miguel and Slovenian Ziga Sesko – the world’s No 1 and No 4 juniors in singles and the top-seeded boys’ doubles team in New York. But when it came to dictating pace, chasing down line drives or the rapid-fire exchanges at net, Davidov never fumbled his racquet.

There were times during his rallies when it was debatable whether a backhand would be easier for him to load or if switching forehand sides mid-rally took some of the edge off when he clearly just wanted to grip and rip. But the double-wing thing is ingrained for Davidov. “I’d say before the main speculation that people had with it, they’d say, I don’t have time to switch hands,” he says. “But I think now as time went on, they kind of see that it’s not a problem. It almost never happens where I’m late for a ball because something goes wrong with the switching.”

On Wednesday, it was a matter of running into a much stronger opponent. Davidov and Lee – wildcard entrants into this draw – had their moments, dazzling the crowd with a handful of pell-mell exchanges, but they were ultimately overwhelmed by Sesko’s punishing groundstrokes and Miguel’s feline reflexes. Sesko, the reigning Australian Open singles and Wimbledon doubles champion, is seriously impressive; Miguel, already a Futures-level title winner, has a real shot at the US Open boys’ singles crown.

For a few early points, Davidov’s unique style appeared to jar them. Occasionally, he can catch players who haven’t faced him before by surprise, “but most of the Americans know me,” he says. Eventually, though, Sesko and Miguel settled into a rhythm and served the Americans a 6-2, 6-2 loss that, while more competitive than the scoreline suggests, spanned 42 minutes nonetheless. “I felt like we were close,” Davidov says. “We just had some loose points, we got broken. I missed a few volleys. But overall it was really fun and really cool to hear the crowd roar after crazy points.”

For Davidov, this trip was about building match experience on the big stage, about properly field-testing his double-wing style. “I’d say the first two days and when I lost my singles, it was so hectic,” he says of his time in New York. “Everything felt like it was going wrong. But I’d say now, especially the last two, three days have been super enjoyable and I’ve gotten used to the courts, which are really fast compared to the ones I play on at home.”

Davidov hasn’t played a ton of juniors events but turned heads in spite of that, last year becoming the first player born in 2010 to pass the qualifying round of a professional M15-level ITF event; that achievement came after he captured the boys doubles title at the prestigious Les Petits As tournament in France. Earlier this year, Davidov reached the semi-finals of an M15 event in Naples to earn his first career ATP points. “To have a guy who can effectively serve left-handed and right-handed at the same level, that is potentially game-changing,” Andy Roddick said on a recent episode of his podcast. “The serving aspect is what really interests me. It’s like having a baseball pitcher who can throw equally well from both sides.” Karue Sell, a professional once ranked as high as No 258 in the world, wondered if he wasn’t looking at the future of tennis after playing Davidov in March.

Really, ever since he began swinging at a suspended ball at age two, Davidov – a Bulgaria native who immigrated to the US young – has been something of an athletic experiment presided over and fiercely protected by his father Kalin and mother Elena – both of whom have backgrounds in sports and holistic medicine. Kalin, a devotee of philosophy and Chinese medicine, devised Teo’s playing style with the goal of creating an athlete who was at one with himself.

“When Teo was about to turn eight years old, I decided he’s going to start playing left-handed, to affect his right hemisphere of the brain,” Kalin told the Guardian in 2021, when his son was 10. “He’s way too extroverted, too fiery, a little too imbalanced, so I just wanted to affect the right hemisphere of his brain, using the left part of his body.”

Many will wince at the routine he was put through while still a child: 30 to 40 hours of training a week, on and off the court – some of it as specialized as exercises focused on breathing through one nostril at a time. These days, Teo says he has added more cardio and weight training to build stamina and fill out a frame that remains a touch on the small side. “Before I was just a little kid, and everyone was twice the size of me and way stronger than me,” he says. “But now I’m kind of growing into my body a bit more.”

Ambidextrous players are the rarest sight in tennis. American Luke Jensen was the last to make a major impression, winning the 1993 French Open doubles title with his younger brother Murphy while ripping 130 mph serves from both wings. And Russia’s Evgenia Kulikovskaya was ranked in the top 100 in the early 2000s while playing tennis with two forehands. The Davidov experiment – he is not naturally ambidextrous – appears to be built on Toni Nadal’s gambit to convert his nephew Rafael from a righty to a leftie, and we all saw how that turned out.

Still, when it comes to the tactical blueprint for Davidov’s game, well, who could serve as a model for a player who is sui generis? “The idea was for the leftie forehand to be more like Rafa and righty to be more like Fed,” Davidov says. “It’s still a work in progress. I don’t know if we’re going to get there someday, but that’s the hope.”

But before you take Davidov for some kind of tennis lab rat, know that his parents have gone to pains to make their boy as well-rounded as those court legends, too. Besides skiing and hiking, Davidov enjoys basketball, American football and soccer. Golf’s the only sport he picked up with two hands. “I used to play left-handed, but I actually switched recently and started playing righty. On the range, it’s definitely going farther.”

After the Open, Davidov said he plans to play a 300-level juniors tournament in Texas before considering a few pro events. As for what lies beyond, he’s still undecided about whether he wants to follow his doubles partner Lee, who’s bound for Duke, and play on a university team (“College [tennis] has gotten so much better lately,” Davidov says) or skip it altogether and turn pro.

Wherever he goes, he’ll remain one to watch – especially if he winds up adding a backhand just to press home his advantage. “We were actually thinking about it, to have even more variety, playing like one point lefty,” he says. “But I think we’re kind of stuck to the two forehands. But we’ll see.”
